subtopic: MR. KNOWLES    CONSIDERATION BY COMMITTEE OF STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR LABELLE

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES    CONSIDERATION BY COMMITTEE OF STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR LABELLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege relates to the fact that this house has been insulted in one way or another, if not in two ways. The basis for my statement is to be found in the remarks, under a question of privilege, that were made yesterday by the hon. member for Labelle. There are two aspects of that statement on which I found my question of privilege today. I shall come to each of them in a moment.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I draw your attention to standing order 79, which reads as follows:
The offer of any money or other advantage to any member of this house for the promoting of any matter whatsoever depending or to be transacted in parliament, is a high crime and misdemeanor, and tends to the subversion of the constitution.
I should like also to draw Your Honour's attention to citation 108, paragraph 5 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads as follows:
The offer of a bribe in order to influence a member in any of the proceedings of the house, or of a committee, has been treated as a breach of privilege, being an insult not only to the member himself, but to the house.
It is the language of that citation that prompted me, in my opening words, to say it is the house that has been insulted. I should like also to draw your attention to section 100 of the Criminal Code of Canada. I shall not read all the section because all of it is not relevant, but I shall read the relevant portion:
Everyone who gives or offers corruptly to a person who holds a judicial office, or is a member of the parliament of Canada or of a legislature, any money, valuable consideration, office, place or employment in respect of anything done or omitted to be done or omitted by him in his official capacity for himself or another person, is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for 14 years.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Labelle, as reported at page 2583 of the English version of Hansard said this:
Mr. Davey was rather suggesting at that moment that I join the ranks of the Liberal party. He said he would take care of the defeated Liberal candidate and as for unsatisfied Liberal organizers, I only would have to change them.
The benefits: a party in power and a fat electoral fund for the next election.

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES    CONSIDERATION BY COMMITTEE OF STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR LABELLE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES    CONSIDERATION BY COMMITTEE OF STATEMENT BY MEMBER FOR LABELLE
speechtext:
The member continued:
Mr. Davey suggested that I ponder those proposals.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Labelle has alleged in this house that he was offered a bribe, that he was offered certain advantages if he would take a certain position in this House of Commons. If that fact is true it is contrary to standing order 79 which I read, to citation 108, paragraph 5 and to section 100 of the Criminal Code.
If this has happened I say it is an insult not just to the hon. member for Labelle but it is an insult to this House of Commons. It is a breach of the privileges of this House of Commons, and the matter certainly ought to be investigated by this house through its committee on privileges and elections.
However, Mr. Speaker, if what the hon. member for Labelle said about things that happened outside this chamber is not true, or even if what he said is true, there is something else in what the hon. member said yesterday which gives offence to this house. It is an insult to one of the members of the house, and therefore is an insult to the house itself. I refer to the very next paragraph in the hon. member's statement, right after the ones I read a moment ago. That next paragraph reads as follows, on the same page 2583 of the English version of yesterday's Hansard:
A week later, a Liberal member of parliament belonging to that same group approached me to tell me that he was very sorry but the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had asked his chief organizer to cease all pressure because he, the Prime Minister, was sure to lose the regular support of the Social Credit party if he ever stole members from that party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that the catcalls that are coming are necessarily any help, but I suggest that those remarks of the hon. member for Labelle, if there is no foundation for them, are an insult to and a calumny upon one of the members of the house, and that member happens to

Question of Privilege
be the Prime Minister. If the Prime Minister, as a member of the House of Commons, has been insulted, again the house itself has been insulted. This was my reason for saying at the outset that the events which have transpired within the last few days have provided one if not two insults to the House of Commons.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in support of my contention that the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle about the Prime Minister are as serious as his allegations with respect to someone outside the house, may I direct your attention to two or three more citations.
First of all, if Your Honour would please look at citation 112 (1) of Beauchesne's fourth edition, you will find it says:
Parliament is not concerned whether or not a libel uttered against it is liable to be tried by a court of law, either of civil or criminal jurisdiction May says: "Both houses will punish not only contempts arising out of facts which the ordinary courts will take cognizance, but those of which they cannot, such as contemptuous insults, gross calumny or foul epithets by word of mouth not within the category of actionable slander or threat of body injury."
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the allegations that have been made are not true, the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Labelle about the Prime Minister come within the terms of that citation.
I also draw your attention to citation 113 in the same volume. This is the citation having to do with questions of privilege, which Your Honour has frequent occasion to read to the house. It is a bit of a text Your Honour uses, and I draw your attention to a sentence in about the middle:
Libels upon members and aspersions upon them in relation to parliament and interference of any kind with their official duties, are breaches of the privileges of the members.
I am relying in particular on the first part of that sentence, which says "Libels upon members and aspersions upon them in relation to parliament" are breaches of the privileges of members. If the statement made by the hon. member for Labelle about the Prime Minister is not true it is a libel upon him in connection with his relationship to parliament, and therefore is a breach of the privileges of parliament.
In the same vein I should like to direct Your Honour's attention to citation 104(5), and in particular to the last sentence in it, at the bottom of page 95 and the top of page 96:
The right of making complaint of a breach of privilege is open to any member of the house, and, even if an individual member alone is affected, is not confined to that member.
In other words, it seems to me that if we look at this as objectively as we can in the light of the concern there is about it, two

members of this house have been insulted. The hon. member for Labelle has been insulted by the alleged offer of a bribe. The Prime Minister has been insulted by what the hon. member for Labelle said about him yesterday.

I am referring to the statement the hon. member for Labelle made to the effect that the Prime Minister stopped the activities of Mr. Keith Davey, not because those activities were wrong but because they interfered with his efforts to retain the support of the Social Credit party. Such a remark, unless it can be substantiated, is an insult and a calumny against the Prime Minister. But my concern is that an insult to any member of the House of Commons is an insult to the house as a whole. That is why I feel this whole matter should be referred to the committee on privileges and elections for a thorough investigation. Such a committee can call witnesses, call those concerned, examine people under oath and get to the bottom of this whole incident.
In a moment or two I will make the appropriate motion which I believe follows from this question of privilege. I have it typed and ready. I have my own name on it as the mover, and my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam is prepared to second it. However, if the Prime Minister himself recognizes the seriousness of this matter, as I am sure he does, and would like to second my motion, my leader would be glad to make way for him.
As regards the whole question of what the house ought to do about this matter, may I direct Your Honour's attention to citation 104(2), which is extremely relevant to the whole question of what is to happen in the next few minutes:
It has often been laid down that the Speaker's function in ruling on a claim of breach of privilege does not extend to deciding the question of substance whether a breach of privilege has in fact been committed-a question which can only be decided by the house itself.
I submit that it would not be using the time of the house properly if we were to debate this type of incident here in this chamber, but we have a committee of this house which could consider the matter and reach a decision. So I hope hon. members will be unanimous in their support of the contention that this matter is so serious that we should not let it drop but should refer it to the appropriate committee. When the dignity of the House of Commons is insulted, as it has been by these developments, we cannot take the matter lightly. Therefore I move:

That the matters raised by the hon. member for Labelle in his question of privilege as reported in Hansard for Monday, April 27, 1964, be referred to the committee on privileges and elections for consideration and report.

subtopic: DECISION NOT TO HOLD CONFERENCE WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschaielels (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: DECISION NOT TO HOLD CONFERENCE WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, immediately preceding the federal-provincial conference recently held in Quebec, and subsequent to it, a number of hon. members, and particularly the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), requested information as to the possibility of a conference with the provincial highways ministers to formulate a national highways policy.
In this regard I would advise the house that the federal government has given consideration to holding a conference with the provincial highways ministers and, as I reported to the house on July 17, 1963, I had made arrangements for certain information to be collected from the provinces on possible programs and expenditures, and in particular to gain a picture of provincial thinking at that stage.
While the federal government has been willing to accept some responsibility in this field, our responsibility has to be examined in relation to the broader division of fiscal responsibility between the federal government and the provinces. The desirability of a federal-provincial conference on highways has therefore to be assessed in relation to the general conference between the federal and provincial governments of last November and the recent one in Quebec.
In the light of the substantial increases in tax transfers to the provincial governments which will result from these conferences, the federal government does not feel it should consider adding at the present time, on a nation-wide basis, to the already

Inquiries of the Ministry very substantial federal contribution to provincial highways. In the circumstances the holding of a federal-provincial conference in the near future would be likely to raise expectations that could not be realized.
The federal government is at present contributing to the cost of highway construction under the Trans-Canada Highway Act until December 31, 1967 and to the roads to resources program. In these programs there is still a substantial and expensive undertaking on the part of the federal government, estimated at this stage to be in the neighbourhood of $240 million.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has he any report to give the house with respect to operations in Cyprus? It would appear that a full scale Greek Cypriot offensive is now under way in the Kyrenia pass headed by the minister of the interior. It would also appear that this has taken place after the Canadian contingent of the United Nations force was unable to get the Turkish Cypriots to vacate their position. Does this mean that this offensive is being undertaken by the Greek Cypriots on behalf of the United Nations, or is the United Nations being ignored in this regard?

maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES PROPOSED TRIP ABROAD BY ROYAL COMMISSION
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-INQUIRIES AS TO ACTIVITIES OF PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend may be assured that no offensive is being taken by the United Nations. The United Nations force is not in Cyprus as an occupational force, nor is it there to further the political purposes or objectives of any one of the groups indigenous to the island.
The fighting to which my hon. friend directs our attention is a new outburst. Over the last week end, fighting was arrested partly as a result of the representations made by the commander of the force to the Cypriot authorities. With regard to the latest incident, I was in touch with the United Nations shortly before coming into the house but I have not got the final details. Until they are in my possession I prefer to make no comment.
In answer to the question my hon. friend asked yesterday, I might say that the Canadian armoured car which, according to reports, was fired upon last week end by Greek Cypriots, was clearly identified by United Nations insignia.

We knew when we went into this enterprise, in pursuance of our obligations under the United Nations charter, that we were undertaking a very difficult assignment. The incidents of the last few days have confirmed the difficulties of this assignment. But that is no reason for putting questions that add to the difficulties of the United Nations force.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose last night we were considering paragraph 7 of the resolution.
Before we go on, I wonder whether the minister has any answers to some of the questions which were put to him on this paragraph last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think what I have said on this paragraph is reasonably clear. At the moment certain fees charged by lawyers, accountants and others in connection with appeals are not allowed as a deductible expense for tax purposes. This provision proposes that they should be allowed as deductible expenses in the same way that similar expenditures by corporations and others are allowed.
The amounts paid will, of course, be included in the income of recipients and tax will be collected on that, so that except in the very few unusual cases, perhaps, where a taxpayer's income is less than the top rates of income of the practitioner, the tax which will .be collected from the practitioner will be higher than the amount of the allowance.
I think last night I answered most of the questions raised by the hon. member. I will be glad to go into this matter again, if he thinks that is necessary.

As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, having raised this objection I would be perfectly prepared to now wait and see the wording of the section in the act; then we could deal with it more fully. We do not know at the moment how the section itself is worded. If it is agreeable to the other members of the committee, I would be perfectly agreeable to moving on. Last night we held paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 in order to obtain further information. Perhaps it would be more orderly if we returned to paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 and proceeded from there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the wish of the committee that we return to paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 to obtain more information from the minister, and return to paragraph 7 later?

Before we leave paragraph 7, Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister a question in order to save time when this legislation is drafted. Paragraph 7 refers to

"any costs". This is not spelled out. Does this refer to lawyers' costs, travelling expenses, and so on; or what does "any costs" mean? Perhaps this will be cleared up in the legislation. There is also nothing in this paragraph which lays down a ceiling; the costs can be as high as they like and there is no ceiling on them. I hope these things will be taken care of in the legislation that is coming forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the costs
referred to here are the legal costs that might be awarded by the court to the taxpayer, and in that event he would have to include those reimbursements as part of his income.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does this conclude the discussion on paragraph 7?

Before we pass from paragraph 7, Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise this matter. The minister has just raised a very interesting point. Is he now suggesting that the only way a taxpayer will be able to recover any of these costs is if they are awarded by a court?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a taxpayer launches an appeal and loses the appeal, it is pretty difficult to think of any other way in which he can recover his costs. By that I mean the amounts he pays out by way of fees. He cannot get them back if he has paid them out and lost his case. If the court finds in his favour and awards him costs at the expense of the crown, then to that extent he gets part of them back.

I said I was satisfied, Mr. Chairman, but I should just like to clarify that one point. I have no particular quarrel with the part of the paragraph dealing with appeals. When we get the section in front of us we can perhaps deal with this matter with greater understanding. I have some real doubts as to the filing of an objection, because this is not an appeal before the court; it is something that is perhaps dealt with in the minister's office, the deputy minister's office, or in the office of the director in Halifax or Vancouver. It is to that point I think the minister should direct his attention very carefully when he sees the section brought in in the bill.

Mr. Chairman, the last two or three remarks of the minister have thrown an altogether different light on the interpretation of what is in paragraph 7. As a matter of fact I think his latest interpretation of how this paragraph will be applied is far superior to the wide range or scope of the interpretation that may have been put on it in the case, for example, of a taxpayer making an appeal against an assessment. I believe that is included in this paragraph, as well as an objection to an assessment. If the minister is now

saying that the application of this paragraph will be confined to costs that are awarded by the court in a case where an appeal is granted, that is considerably different than the interpretation we took from his remarks yesterday.
Mr. Chairman, can the minister assure us that these costs will only be costs that might be awarded by a court?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; the proposal is that the amount of the fees paid, which may be in excess of the amount of costs settled by the court, should be allowed as a deductible expense. But I think last night I referred to the particular section of the act, section 12 (2), which permits the department to disallow anything that might be unreasonable.
I have one other point. Will the income tax appeal board be granted the authority to assess costs in cases of this nature?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, according to clause 7, I appreciate that the taxpayer can deduct from his income the amounts he had to pay in order to appeal against a judgment or a decision by an income tax assessor.
Now, when a taxpayer is faced with court action by officials of the Department of Finance or the Department of National Revenue, sometimes it costs him a lot of money to pay his lawyers. Does the government intend to assume such expenses when the taxpayer wins his case, which would prove that the government employees were completely wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have not thought of anything that goes that far, although if it went so far as to get before the exchequer court or the supreme court and that court saw fit to award costs to the taxpayer, then he would recoup them to that extent; but not in an appeal to an official of the department or to the tax appeal board.

I do not want to belabour this matter, Mr. Chairman, but I just want to clarify one point. Then there is no possibility of a taxpayer being able to claim any part of the costs involved in objecting to an appeal-that is, for accountants' or lawyers' fees, or anything of that nature-in a case that went only as far as one of the officials of the department or even the tax appeal board? It would have to go beyond that, to the exchequer court or the Supreme Court of Canada, before he would be able to make any claim from his taxable income with respect to the costs of so doing?
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that we have become a little mixed up with this word "costs". The kind of costs that my hon. friend referred to I would like to call expenses. Those legal expenses or other expenses, under this section, will be allowed as deductions from the taxpayer's income whether or not he wins the case. If, however, he goes further, to the exchequer court or the supreme court, wins his case and the judgment includes what are known as costs, this paragraph means he is reimbursed for his legal fees. Then, if having been allowed to deduct the legal fees in the first place, he gets them paid back to him by the crown, he has to include what he receives as income. In other words he cannot have it both ways.

Mr. Chairman, there still seems to be some confusion about this. Let us take the case of a constituent of mine who objects to his assessment. He goes as far as he can with the local officials; then he comes to Ottawa and spends a week here, possibly with counsel, and debates the matter with the officials of the Department of National Revenue. Can he deduct the cost to which he has been put? Is it a deductible item in the preparation of his income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, absolutely. The last phrase refers to something else altogether. But in the example given by the hon. member he would be entitled to deduct from his taxable income his total expenses in connection with his representations to the department. That is the point about which my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings has some doubt, I think, but according to the resolution all the expenses incurred by a constituent from London going to Ottawa, with counsel or anybody else he might like to take with him, will be allowed as a deduction from his taxable income.
Does that apply whether or not he wins his point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, whether or not he wins. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, as an example, a taxpayer files his income tax return in which he claims, let us say, a sum of $700 as charitable donations. The department decides to cut down this sum and reduce it to $200, and does so arbitrarily as usual. The taxpayer then asks the services of a lawyer to plead his case and substantiate the amount claimed as charitable donations. Will all the expenses thus incurred by the taxpayer be deductible for income tax purposes, whether he wins or loses his case?

If he is arguing about an amount of $300 and his lawyer charges him $500, he can deduct the $500 from his income but he still has to pay the lawyer $500. So there is a pretty good check on this.

Mr. Chairman, for a number of weeks now we have been endeavouring to get some correct information from the ministry with respect to industries which have established themselves in designated areas for the purpose of availing themselves of the incentives proposed by the government. In all these efforts we have not as yet been able to get anything definite either from the Minister of Industry or from the Minister of Finance; all we get is a conglomeration of words and answers which are not directly related to the questions asked.
As an example of this, Mr. Chairman, a written question put by the hon. member for Peterborough was replied to on April 13. The hon. member asked five questions and I will refer only to the first, which is reported at page 2078 of Hansard. It is as follows:
1. How many industries have settled in the designated areas since these areas were set up?
This is a question which is quite simple and understandable. It is asking how many industries have settled. Let us take a look at the reply which the hon. member received from the Minister of Industry:
1. Thirty four new businesses are being established in Canada-
The question asked how many have settled, and the answer is that 34 are being established in Canada. The answer is not in conformity with the question put. Then yesterday the Minister of Finance, as reported at page 2632 of Hansard, made this statement:
[Mr. Caouette.l

I am informed that 150 proposals for new businesses have been discussed with the area development agency. Of these over 40 companies have formally indicated they are going ahead with projects to be located in 14 of the 35 designated areas.
Then at the conclusion of his remarks the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings asked the minister:
Could the minister give us the geographical areas involved in these applications? I do not want them by counties but how many are there, for instance, in the Atlantic provinces and how many in Ontario, Quebec and the west?
There is nothing difficult to answer there. The minister replied as follows:
The Minister of Industry informs me that an answer was given today and will appear in Hansard tor today. I do not have the answer before me.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have searched vainly in Hansard of yesterday's date to which the minister referred, but no answer appears to have been given. This is just an indication either of evasiveness on the part of ministers or a lack of knowledge as to what is happening. As I say, we have searched Hansard without success, failing to find the answer which according to the minister was given.
Then the Minister of Industry got into the act a little later on, and amongst other things he said, as reported at page 2633 of Hansard:
These 40 industries in 14 of the 35 designated areas are planning capital investments-
Then he went on to give the amounts. Surely the government, through the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Industry, can tell us in fairly wide terms where these 40 industries are establishing, or have established, themselves. I do not think any industries have established themselves in Canada yet in any of these designated areas, because I followed this matter up and asked this question of the Minister of Industry yesterday, as reported at the same page of Hansard:
Will the minister tell us now how many have been actually established? Has there been one, have there been four or has there been none?
I am sure that yesterday the Minister of Industry said there were none, yet in Hansard this answer appears:

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production

I do not think that there is one that has come into commercial operations yet.
That is the sort of answer, Mr. Chairman, which we get to a specific question. I asked the minister whether he would tell us how many industries have been actually established. Again I got an evasive answer, although I do not think the minister uttered the words which appear in Hansard because I am fairly certain he said none. But according to Hansard he said:

I do not think that there is one that has come into commercial operations yet.
In view of all this confusion and evasiveness-and all we in this committee are trying to do is find out the facts-surely if none has been established yet the government ought to be honest and aboveboard and say so. I suggest that we stop all this beating about the bush with words, because I think we would get on much more quickly if the answers were direct and to the point.

paragraph 4. Will the minister explain to the committee this reference to the fair market value? Does this mean that a manufacturer can use second hand machinery now, whereas before he had to use new machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of the proposal in the resolution is precisely the opposite. As the law now stands the use of capital goods for used machinery can be manipulated and a large quantity of second hand equipment could be bought from a parent company at a very slight capital cost, and a business may qualify by equipping with very little new machinery. There would be no advantage to this. In order to prevent this manipulation, the resolution proposes to substitute fair market value of assets in place of the written down value of capital cost in the application which is now found under section 71A(3). In this test it is provided that a company does not qualify unless 95 per cent of the machinery, equipment and buildings owned or leased and used in the business are situated in the designated area. It can be got around by a little ingenuity, and I think that is the kindest word I could use at the moment. This section is designed to prevent that.
Paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall we go to paragraph 8?
On paragraph 8.

I should like to ask the minister to give us an explanation of paragraph 8, which is a very technical one. It is one, I am sure, for which he can give us an adequate explanation so that we can understand the technical language.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this proposes a broadening of the rules concerning the deduction of amounts contributed by employees into a registered pension plan. It proposes an amendment to allow an employee to deduct an amount contributed in respect of services in past years while he was a contributor to a plan, even though he may also claim a deduction for the same years in respect of services in past years while he was not a contributor. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to cover a situation where a member of a pension plan wants to make a lump sum or annual contribution in respect of services for previous years, during some of which he was a contributor and during some of which he was not a contributor. The intention is to smooth out or to clarify the situation where some individuals are being discriminated against.

I did not understand what the minister meant when he referred to past years. Before I come to that, I gather that the reference to any previous year since 1962 means that in computing his income an amount may be deducted in 1963 or subsequent years; am I right in that? If a taxpayer were to file a claim against 1963, which presumably has been filed, this would
Income Tax Act
be taken into consideration. The minister said, "During past years while he was a contributor and while he was not a contributor." I presume he is going to make a lump sum payment to cover the period while he was not a contributor, or distributed over a period of time, related to that period when he was not a contributor. Is he presumed to be making that payment on that period now, or increasing the payments for that period?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has been suggested to me that instead of trying to give a short and snappy answer to that question I should explain what the present law is. The law at present permits an employee to claim a deduction for a contribution into a registered pension plan under three principal subparagraphs. The first deals with current services, not exceeding $1,500 a year in respect of such current services; the second is for past services, not exceeding $1,500 a year in respect of services in past years while he was not a contributor. If an amount in excess of $1,500 is contributed under this subparagraph in a year, the excess may be carried forward and deducted in subsequent years.
Now, the third provision also has to do with past services. It applies if an employee has not made a deduction under the second provision. He may deduct an amount in respect of services in past years while he was a contributor; and the amount deducted in a year under this subparagraph, plus the amount deducted under the first subparagraph for current services may not exceed $1,500. This means an employee may deduct a maximum of $3,000 under these various provisions. The deduction under the second one is intended to cover the employee who did not join a pension plan of his employer at the commencement of his employment, but in later years wants to make a contribution for those years of employment while he was not a contributor. The deduction under subparagraph (3) is intended to cover an employee who wishes to increase the contributions he made in previous years. The proposed change would permit an employee to make a deduction in respect of services in past years while he was not a contributor, even though he also deducts an amount in the year in respect of services in past years while he was not a contributor. The maximum amount deductible in respect of past years while he was a contributor shall not exceed $1,500, minus the amount deductible in a year, (a) on account of current services and (b) on account of services in past years while he was not a contributor-

Would the minister repeat that last line, minus the amount-

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Minus the amount deducted in a year (a) on account of current services in past years while he was not a contributor.
Now, I thoroughly agree with other members of the committee that this is a rather complicated subject. The purpose is to allow people to pay up their past contributions if they so wish, and not to hinder them in the process.
Is the total amount that he may deduct in any one year still $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is correct. It can never be more than $3,000.
But he may distribute it in different categories?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
This was intended to be a relieving section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I might say, if it has any bearing on the situation, that there is a member of the committee who is not here today who comes into a category described by the minister, being in the employment of one of the very large corporations of this country, and he was told by his personnel officer that he would be penalized by the passing of this paragraph. The hon. member is not here today, but presumably he will be present when the bill comes before the house. At that stage he may have some questions concerning his own personal status, but the minister says this is a relieving section and in no way penalizes those within any of these categories.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings would be kind enough to speak to his friend so that I might have an opportunity of having a word with him before the bill comes forward.
I will do that.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 9.

This is an interesting paragraph, especially in view of the fact that the Department of National Revenue has been endeavouring to encourage Canadians to pay their taxes as early as possible following the end of the calendar year. If further payments are to be made into a registered pension plan over a period of 120 days from the end of the year, it is only natural that taxpayers will wait for receipts from a pension fund, and this will further crowd the filing of returns into the last 30 days before returns are generally due. Will an individual, who may be paying
[Mr. Monteith.I
into a pension plan, be allowed 120 days along with employers, or will he just be cut off at the end of the 60 day period? At present this paragraph states specifically that the extension to 120 days applies only to employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The intention is that this would only be extended to employers because the individual has a fixed amount he has to pay, and he knows what it is. In some of the corporation pension plans the amount a corporation pays in is dependant to some extent on its profits for the year. It may pay a certain amount plus a percentage of its profits, and in some cases it has been said that corporations do not know what their profits are 60 days after the end of the year.
There are some companies which take a little longer than others in closing their books, and it has proven to be impossible for them to determine what they owe to a pension plan within a period of two months. So they need longer in order to ascertain the exact amount.

I thank the minister for that explanation, but it is equally true that some commercial salesmen for insurance companies, and other individuals working for large corporations, are not aware of the amount of commission or bonus that may be forwarded to them. If their bonus is late in arriving they may wish to lower their own income tax by making a heavier contribution to a pension plan, and it would be only fair that this provision, if it is extended to large corporations, should also be extended to all Canadians so that there would be no discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There may be something in what the hon. gentleman says, although I am informed that there have been no representations and no complaints on this point. I would prefer to inquire into it to see if there is a real difficulty before taking it into account. I must say I am sympathetic with the point that has been made, and it is the sort of thing we might look into next year. However, I would like to be sure that there is some substance to it.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 10.

I am assuming that actually the intent now is that any amount received by an employer upon the winding up or reorganization of a pension fund or plan shall be included in his income in the year it is received. I understand there has apparently been some weakness discovered in the present bill, and that this amendment is purely to make sure that this is so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct, Mr. Chairman. In one court case, which I think brought hope

to the hearts of others, it was ruled that when a pension plan was wound up and there was a surplus in it which came back to the corporation, the corporation did not have to pay tax on the amount it received in this fashion. This was a windfall and the corporation got off scot free. It was brought to the attention of the government and it was decided that this was something that should not be allowed to continue.

I am wondering about the wording of the paragraph. I can understand that on the winding up of any pension plan the amount left should be taken into income, but I can conceive where in the reorganization of a pension fund this would not be fair or advisable. I was wondering whether it should not be worded to read "shall be" on the winding up and "may be" on the reorganization of a pension plan, in order to permit some discrimination to the officials administering the act, rather than to make it mandatory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would only be taxable if the corporation received the money. After all, the corporation would have been allowed this as a deduction in earlier years when the amounts were paid into the pension fund. If, at any time, it gets that money back it should pay tax on it, and I think it would apply to reorganization as well as winding up.
I could imagine a reorganization where it would be just a transfer, where it really does not become vested in the corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This would only apply if it became vested in the corporation.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 11.
Would the minister give us an explanation of this paragraph? I think he said yesterday that it is a technical one to clarify the act. I would like to have the explanation again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the proposed change an expense that becomes owing in a year will be deductible in that year, but if the amount is not actually paid within two years from the end of the year in question-the end of the year in which it becomes owing -the taxpayer who has taken the deduction must add the amount back into his income in the third year unless he, and the person to whom the amount is owing, file a certain election.
In this election the debtor and creditor must agree that the taxes should be computed as though the debt had been repaid and replaced by a loan. If such an election is filed,
Income Tax Act
the amount owing shall be deemed to be paid in the third year and returned to the debtor as a loan.
I would like to give an illustration of this. If the taxpayer claims a deduction for interest which is payable to somebody else, the "somebody else" does not pay any tax on the interest until he receives it. The first taxpayer can claim a deduction at present even though he does not pay it.
It is suggested there are cases where the crown is short-changed, if I may use that expression, in this way, and if that particular interest charge is not actually paid within three years it has to be brought back into the income of the original taxpayer who obtained a deduction in the first year. I do not suggest this is a major loophole, but it is certainly a mousehole.
What if the taxpayer pays it in a subsequent year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then he gets the credit for it. He gets the reduction once, not twice.
Yes, but if he takes it back into income he is paying tax on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then when he gets around to paying it he is allowed to deduct it.
He gets it back at that time.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 12.

There are a few references I intend to make regarding this matter and, of course, I intend to seek information from the minister respecting some observations made very recently by United States under secretary George Ball who spoke on United States-Canada economic relations last Saturday night.
I should like to find out from the minister what his views are on the speech which was delivered-a speech which he tabled following a request on my part that he do so yesterday.
I begin by referring to the transcript of the program "Conversation with the Prime Minister" on Sunday, April 19, wherein the Prime Minister, speaking with political modesty, referred to a clipping from a newspaper correspondent in Washington which said that Canadian-United States relations are better today than they have been in years-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Good.

The finance minister applauds. I merely direct attention to that. I take it that, in keeping with the attitude adopted by all ministers of this government, any statement made by the Prime Minister,

Income Tax Act
regardless of whether they agree with it or not, is the object of approbation and loud applause.
Now I intend to refer, first, to the Canadian Press dispatch in which Mr. Ball is reported as referring to key economic policies of the Canadian government-I refer to the dispatch in the narrative form.
He said that in a situation such as that of Canada and the U.S., with closely intertwined economic affairs and large trade, "any change in the existing ground rules can have immediate and substantial repercussions".
Then he went on to list the various things which could cause what he called repercussions:
Measures designed to induce a change in the character of foreign investment from equity to debt.
Measures designed to "refuse national treatment to capital that had earlier been welcomed."
There is no indirectness about those two criticisms or statements. They have to do with action taken by the present government. The third is:
Measures to bring about the transfer of production from one country to another.
That criticism, too, is levelled directly against the present government which, when in opposition paraded itself as the friend of good relations with the United States and criticized us for what we had done in order to maintain Canada's individuality. At that time hon. gentlemen now sitting opposite condemned us for endeavouring to assure that our resources in the north, controlled by the Canadian government, should as far as possible be available for investment by Canadians. Having made those criticisms, the very first action taken by the present government was the threat of the 30 per cent tax-about which I do not intend to say more-and the subsequent retreat, and then the further action which Mr. Ball criticizes in his remarks. Then the article goes on to say:
Canadian finance minister Walter Gordon, in a speech before the New York Economic Club last Monday, said Canada would like to see an increasing proportion of foreign investment in Canada "in the form of loans which can be paid off."
And it continues:
Ball's second point, about refusal of national treatment to capital that had earlier been welcomed, appeared to refer to Canadian action to increase Canadian financial participation in U.S.-owned subsidiaries.
The third point on transfer of production ran counter to statements by Gordon in New York that Canada would have to increase its exports of manufactured goods to the U.S. to cope with its current account deficit.
Then the report describes this speech as having a "rough and tough quality"-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was not my speech.

No, not the speech of the hon. gentleman, whose suavity can never be described in those terms. He believes in saccharine words, and then he withdraws. Not so, Mr. Ball. Mr. Ball's speech had a rough and ready quality-in the words of the article, it was "a reminder of what America could or could not do to help Canada". Then he went on to deal with Canada's general attitude, and he dealt, also, with some bitterness-never does the Minister of Finance, and I pause to say this, allow any of his words to be saturated with bitterness; I am speaking of the Canadian Press description of Mr. Ball's berating of the government of Canada-he spoke with bitterness of "Ottawa proposals to discourage Canadian companies from advertising in American magazines which circulate in Canada, as a form of protection". Then he added:
I would hope that however the Canadian government may ultimately resolve this question it will not act in such a manner as to inhibit the free flow of thought across our borders.
His observations in this direction were, of course, entirely motivated by a commendable desire to ensure that Canadians should not deny themselves the opportunity of a full and complete education in world matters. Then the report says:
Mr. Ball's speech reflected a Washington apprehension that in its century-old desire to maintain a Canadian identity and amidst a growing tension among French Canadians in Quebec seeking greater autonomy or even separatism, Ottawa may adopt policies to counter what the state department regards as the inevitable spread of "economic interdependence" between the two countries.
There is something here with which we are all of us in agreement. In a concluding report, the American assembly, to which this speech was delivered "decided the United States should not try to bind Canadian foreign policies into a pattern of conformity with United States policies". That was tried in connection with the trade and commerce of this country in non-strategic materials during the days when we were in office-and tried unsuccessfully.
What I wish to find out from the minister is this: Has he made any representations as yet, to Mr. Ball? It is going to be difficult for him to do so, because when there was that great interference by the state department with political issues in Canada in January of 1963 it was those hon. members who sit opposite, now on the treasury benches, who approved of gross interference in matters of Canadian domestic concern. I am interested to know whether there has been any change in the viewpoint of the government in this connection. Does the minister accept this stark,

harsh criticism even described by the Canadian Press as rough and tough? Does he accept this? We would like to be let in on some of the representations the Canadian government is making in this regard. It is said, "Sharp issue has been taken with this government's fiscal and economic policies". The opposition has taken sharp issue with some of these policies which were entirely ill-digested, ill-conceived and had to be withdrawn by the Minister of Finance and those associated with him.
We ask, what is the approach, because it was quite a remarkable speech that was delivered. It dealt with cultural infiltration. He holds out some hope for Canada in this regard, because he says:
I am aware of the apprehensions in some circles that Canada risks being culturally overwhelmed by the United States. We Americans are a vocal, sometimes a rather noisy, people, and the development of radio and television has extended exposure to American cultural influence beyond the written to the spoken word.
Then he is disturbed about the press-I have referred to that already-being interfered with in any way, as he said. Then he referred to the areas of complexity and said:
The areas of greatest complexity and difficulty between our two nations lie in the range of our commercial and economic policies.
He pointed out that there is really no criticism that the United States has tariffs high enough to keep our products out of the United States, while our tariffs practically render available competition from any part of the world. He says this:
But what is often forgotten is that on a per capita basis Canadians have invested almost twice as much in the United States as Americans have in Canada.
That is just one of the old dodges regarding the use of statistics, which is not applicable in any way to the situation that prevails. He said:
From the point of view of economic principles, there is no doubt that Canada and the United States could employ the resources of North America most efficiently by developing the continent as a single great market.
Indeed, he goes so far as to suggest that we should get together. He would not be much concerned with divisions between our countries. We have resources that they need, and therefore everything should be done, as he said, to move toward commercial liberalization. He said it is hopeful that we will move even farther in that direction, although some of us have drawn back, for political reasons, from the ultimate logic of the single market. Then he deals with the minister and he really gives him the works. It was obvious yesterday that the minister realized he had got the full treatment. The minister does not 20220-170
Income Tax Act
always smile when he gets the full treatment, but he is smiling on this occasion because he cannot do otherwise; he is going to meet Mr. Ball tomorrow. Mr. Ball said:
But difficulties necessarily arise when the anxiety to avoid economic interdependence leads to policies that are discriminatory and inequitable.
That is his description of the economic policies of this government:
This is particularly the case with close neighbours such as the United States and Canada-
Then he goes on to say this:
-any change in existing ground rules can have immediate and substantial repercussions. Measures by governments designed to induce a change in the character of investment from equity to debV-
That was the minister's own suggestion only a day or so before:
-for example, or to refuse national treatment to capital that had earlier been welcomed, or to bring about the transfer of production from one country to another can be seriously disruptive.
The minister cannot accept that, if he remains true to the ever nescient policies that he enunciated in June and July last, and since. I want to hear what his reaction is to this. I know that someone said some of his policies were pre-Keynesian. Some of them are pre-Cambrian. Mr. Ball takes it upon himself to teach the Canadian government a lesson. He said:
The desire of our Canadian friends to safeguard the identity of their national market apparently stems from the belief that the nation and people may lose something of their national political independence if their economy is too closely meshed with that of other nations and particularly the United States.
I do not think we have ever got a more complete lesson from the administration of the United States on what Canada should do than Mr. Ball gave vent to the other day. Then he said:
Certainly, neither Canada nor the United States is interested in yielding or compromising its own freedom of political decision... I do not believe, therefore, that as between Canada and the United States there is any basis for assuming an automatic and parallel relation between increased economic interdependence and a loss of independence in political life.
Now, sir, I want to hear from the minister what is his reaction to this. Does he share the fulsome terms that were used in criticism by him and his associates, when in January and February, 1963 the state department of the United States chose to issue a document giving information such as the one in question here issued by the United States information service? Will the minister tell the committee what is the attitude of the government in this connection? When we were in office we were criticized regarding our attitude toward preserving Canada's right to declare her policies within Canada, while

Income Tax Act
maintaining the fullest co-operation with the other legions of freedom and the other nations of freedom. We were criticized by the Liberal party and they said we were antiAmerican. I want to know from the minister now, has he in the course of one year turned a somersault, too, in the views regarding the matters that he expressed a year ago-because it will not be unusual. He will not be alone if he admits he has turned a somersault; he will have company all down the front bench. I want to know, has he changed his views in this regard?
Do you remember, Mr. Chairman, how they criticized us with regard to American investment. Will the minister tell us what American investment came into Canada between last October and December, those three months, and during January, February and March of this year. We would like to get the figures; we have never had the official figures for the last three months of 1963. We know that when we were in office American investment in Canada, in the last two three-month periods, amounted to $400 million. We know that in that third quarter of 1963 that amount had fallen, under this government, with its tinkering, its economic nonsense in the manner in which it brought these policies into effect. We wanted to bring about Canadian strength, not through the club but through incentives, and that is what we did. That is the reason we were able to assure a continuance of investment.
Four hundred million dollars was the average for the last two three-month periods of our tenure of office. In the third quarter of 1963 it was down to $98 million. That is my understanding, on the basis of the figures that I have, although I do not say they are correct. It is a matter of computation that we have not been able to get. The amount is down to something like $60 million, I understand. I ask the minister before this item is passed to give us the figures of American investment in Canada in the last three months of 1963 and the first three months of 1964. If he cannot give us the first three months, he can give us the first two months, which will show that as a result of the economic fallacy that was his and those associated with him they have destroyed or reduced almost to a trickle the investment in our country.
Why? Simply because of the uncertainty of investors in Canada. They do not know what will be the next tinkering in which the Minister of Finance will indulge himself. Nobody knows. The minister started by chopping away, decided that he would discontinue his chopping and changed to a smaller axe. But the effect is just the same. We want to know what is his attitude in this regard. Why is it 
that there has not been on his part greater emphasis on incentives, rather than on pressure and the infliction of what we described as discriminatory reactions on the part of this government? We want to know whether, if paragraph 12 is passed, this will be the last tinkering which will be done. Countries everywhere want to invest in Canada.
When the Conservative government was in office the Liberal party of that day said that we had discouraged investment. However, since they have been in power investment has gone down and down, and more than one minister has gone on bended knee to Washington in order to engage in dialogue with Washington to implore, as it were, an increase in the amount of investment. The minister even admitted the other day that foreign investment must continue. If we require foreign investment, then what is going to be done to encourage it? We believe in foreign investment. We never altered our view in that regard. But we stated that while investment was welcomed, investment in Canada should be used by the corporations for the benefit of Canada generally rather than be put at the direction of a country elsewhere, however friendly. That was our view and our stand, and we maintained that United States investment in Canada should become Canadianized.
What has happened today? First, the government brought in a series of experiments. Bold and imaginative, was the expression of the Prime Minister. They were bold, but they were so unimaginative that the government had to withdraw them one by one. Now the latest retreat is in this particular piece of legislation. How the government rushed to increase the percentage from 15 to 20. This was the salvation, said the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. Now after a few months they come back to parliament and say: "It is just another mistake which we made". No; they do not admit that: It is the result of dialogue. That is the expression today.
We want to hear something of this dialogue between the Minister of Finance and other ministers with United States cabinet secretaries. What has happened? What representation has been made? What is the general attitude of the government? Is it a protectionist attitude? How the Liberal party used to condemn us for a protectionist attitude. I would point out that no longer are we condemned for that. Instead the present government's own press gives it almost universal condemnation for its uncertain, irregular, ill-conceived policies which have been effective in one respect only, and that is in having

parliament pass these measures, only to be asked a few months later to reverse their decision.
We want to know, why this reversal. Why are they swallowing themselves on that side of the house? The "medicine" which was prescribed eight, nine or ten months ago was not mixed hurriedly. It was all set out in the pharmacopoeia of "Troubled Canada". When was it discovered that the beneficial medicine which was so effective when it was first prescribed in that masterful work has turned out to be poison? These are matters about which we should like to know. I realize the minister is just waiting for the opportunity to furnish this information, and I want to give him a full opportunity.
I mentioned a moment ago that even the minister's best friends are criticizing him. You would not think, Mr. Chairman, that even they would tell him. "Even your best friends won't tell you", is how one ad reads. But the minister's best friends are telling him today. This is what the Winnipeg Free Press said on March 28:
Canada's attitude toward trading relationships between the industrialized and the underdeveloped countries of the world was outlined to the United Nations world trade and development conference in Geneva this week by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Paul Martin.
Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs is given praise, although we are told that he may indeed be considering leaving us shortly to assume a very high position; at least that is the rumour which is going around in the international field. The article continues:
Mr. Martin was moderate and cautious in tone-
He does not always show it in the house, but apparently he was on this occasion.
-but his remarks were sufficiently liberal to take some of the curse off the restrictionist, defensive approach implicit in Mr. Gordon's 1964 budget speech.
The Free Press have always worshipped at the throne of Liberalism and been intense admirers of both the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. Yet the policies of this government were described as restrictionist and defensive approaches. Then the article continues in these words:
Canadians who believe that their prosperity depends on greatly expanded international trade have been disturbed at the lukewarm approach to trade shown by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. Mr. Martin's contribution to the U.N. conference must give rise to hopes that Mr. Gordon is not the voice of the government at Ottawa, but only of a small minority. Whether these hopes are justified will be answered-
__and so on. The general conclusion is
that this government, pretending that it is following one policy, has become a restrictive, and I would add discriminatory, gov-20220- 1704

ernment. We want to know why the change. What has happened? Is it actually redemption that has been bought by this government? Last year they said that these things had to be done. They told us that this section raising the percentage from 15 to 20 represented a tremendous step forward. Now the government say: "We are going to depart from it". Mr. Chairman, my time is up.

the second reading of Bill No. C-19, with respect to hospital and university sweepstakes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words in favour of the proposal before us, I must make it clear at the outset that I speak for myself and not for my party. I personally regret this. In the New Democratic party we have a lot of very high principles and admirable moral and ethical ideals which I certainly share, but sometimes I feel members of the New Democratic party, like the members of labour movements, and perhaps socialist movements in other countries, are at times apt to be in the order of the old Roundheads of Puritan days, and are apt to take a rather Puritan point of view as to some of the facts of life.
This is in contrast to some of those around about us, those who belong to the older parties, and who are much more like the Cavalier types than the Puritan Roundheads. Having this in mind I think it is possible for me, on my own behalf, to say a word or two in favour of the principle of legalizing sweepstakes, in the same way as it was possible for some of the sober Roundheads to cast an admiring glance at Nell Gwyn, and who were none the worse for it. Speaking as one who favours public control and public operation of sweepstakes provincially as in the public interest, I want to put forward five facts which underline what seems to me the need for this legislation.
First, the question today is actually not whether we want sweepstakes. We have sweepstakes. It is estimated that no less than 28 sweepstake operations of a major nature are functioning in Canada at this time. Gambling and drinking are two of the oldest human frailties of which we have record. Drawing by lot, which is a form of gambling, is favourably recorded in the Old Testament, in Joshua chapter 18 verse 10. In the case of drinking, the public long ago gave up the idea that it could, through prohibition, be legislated out of existence.
We have public control of drinking, with the public contributing to the government, through taxation, a considerable amount of the public drinking money. My contention is that the time has come, indeed it is long overdue, to apply the same general principle
Sweepstakes
to the control of sweepstakes in Canada, just as we have done earlier with gambling at the race tracks.
My second point is that at present, as previous speakers have mentioned, millions of dollars leave this country every year to subsidize the private or public sweepstake promoters in other countries. Legislation permitting a provincial or national sweepstake would reduce this toll, and keep a good deal of this money in Canada.
My third fact is that the most modest estimate of sweepstake revenue on a provincial basis indicates that a province, say the size of British Columbia with the population of British Columbia, would net over $1 million a year. This in effect would be a do-it-yourself tax paid by the sweepstake participants. In time to come, United States tourists would add their money to a British Columbia sweepstake, at no cost to our taxpayers. The proceeds would be sufficient, I estimate, to build at least one chronic hospital every 12 months in British Columbia, something which hon. members will agree is very badly needed there.
My fourth point is that Canada is one of the dwindling number of countries which do not already have some form of national, provincial, or government lottery. Countries with as divergent policies as Great Britain and the Soviet union have, if not a sweepstake in the terms of the Irish sweepstake, at least a government bond lottery through which- and I may say I have one here-a person may buy a non-interest bearing bond and thereby be a participant in a draw which distributes a number of prizes to lucky ticket holders. The public is thereby, as it is also in the U.S.S.R., encouraged to invest in state enterprises and the state saves the interest it would otherwise have to pay. A side beneficial effect of this policy is a reduction in inflationary tendencies by the siphoning off of this amount of money into government enterprises.
There are now 30 countries which have sweepstakes or lotteries of one type or another, including New Zealand which has already been mentioned, where the popularity of these enterprises is now so great that they have several every year.
Fifth, I would urge action to regularize sweeps on a basis of respect for the law. Our present anti-sweepstake law is flouted daily by thousands of Canadians, and has been for many years. It is time to make a law that conforms to public usage in this matter rather than to strive vainly to make the public conform to this outdated and unworkable law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have a lawyer's qualifications to determine the most efficient way to operate lotteries in the various Canadian provinces. Neither do I intend to discuss the legal aspects thereof, nor suggest the legal procedure best suited for amending the Criminal Code to authorize the operation of provincial lotteries. But I want to express my humble opinion on the subject matter of Bill No. C-19.
Like the hon. member who preceded me, I want to say that I am only expressing my personal opinion and do not want to commit anybody in my group. Though we are but few, it might happen that one or the other would disagree with me.
I therefore want to say that I am in favour of the principle that the Criminal Code be amended so as to enable the provinces which want to do so, to operate the lotteries as considered necessary within their respective territories.
I would even go further than the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), the mover of Bill No. C-19, by not limiting provincial governments as to quantity or method of disposing of the funds thus collected.
When the matter of lotteries is considered, a moral problem is encountered and many people cut short any discussion of the subject by putting up a screen of ethics. But, meanwhile, lottery tickets of all kinds are sold and bought at an ever-increasing rate.
Besides, those lotteries, unfortunately, are organized most of the time by people whose honesty and integrity are more than questionable. No control is possible on the way prizes are drawn, and most of the sums of money collected in this way go into the already full pockets of certain professional parasites.
In my opinion, the question has already been sufficiently considered, at least enough to enlighten us, the legislators, on the urgency of revising our stand on that matter and protecting, as far as possible, the interests of those who elected us.
The newspapers, throughout the country, conducted thorough investigations on lotteries, obtaining in the process opinions from hundreds of thousands of readers who, in over 90 per cent of the cases, said they were in favour of the organization of such lotteries and of amending the Criminal Code, in order to allow provincial governments to establish their own lotteries.
I am sure a great proportion of the people would be glad to take part in lotteries, which they would know in advance to be organized 

by responsible people, with everything aboveboard and with the proceeds payable to charitable organizations.
In certain quarters, they state it is bad, and even immoral to participate in lotteries, but they do nothing to put an end to it. I believe that with provincial lotteries an end would be put to lots of small organizations, unfortunately controlled by people whose only aim is to exploit a simple-minded public. I do not say that all present organizations are actually in the hands of dishonest people, for there are sweepstakes the philanthropic aim of which is well recognized and the administration of which is perfectly honest.
If we allowed the establishment of such provincial lotteries, we could make use at home, for purposes equally noble, of large amounts of dollars we are presently exporting.
For those reasons, I say it is urgent to legislate in order to stop this hemorrhage of funds which go to help foreign organizations and which could serve right purposes.
In my opinion, it is time the government took its own responsibilities to meet the situation and legislated accordingly. There exists also an evil which should be recognized, I admit. It is perhaps not an argument to put forward, but I know many people have not got the means to buy these lottery tickets but, in view of the existing evil, of two evils should we not choose the lesser.
That is why I believe it is urgent for our legislation to be directed in such a way as to serve the well-being of the population.
Is it not our duty as representatives of the people to pass the pieces of legislation that they want? Is it not our responsibility to reflect here the opinion of our constituents? I believe that is our most definite mandate. That is why, even if I do not completely agree with the provisions of Bill No. C-19, I must nevertheless support it, considering that it is a first step in the right direction.
If I wanted to take this opportunity to play politics, like the hon. members for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), and Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), I would say that if the government is now trying by every possible means to get the necessary revenues in order to meet all its objectives, if governments at all levels are faced with many financial problems they cannot solve, they should apply the monetary policies that we advocate. In brief, they would find them a much more effective remedy than the setting up of lotteries.

Mr. Speaker, I trust that before I finish my remarks on this bill the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gr6-goire) will recognize that, while I agree in principle that something should be done about this problem of lotteries in Canada, I have the common sense to oppose with every justification the passage of this particular bill on the subject. During the debate the hon. and distinguished gentleman from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) included some gratuitous observations about the state of this government. He referred in rather extravagant terms, without any foundation whatsoever, to the fact that we in this country were heading for bankruptcy. He very smoothly passed over the deficit spending of prior years, and as is sometimes the case with narrow-minded people he was looking through a keyhole with both of his eyes. I am sure that he was not serious when he made these gratuitous additions to what was otherwise a reasoned debate in favour of an amendment to the Criminal Code to permit lottery operations.
During the course of the debate another hon. member referred to the extensive volume of dollars which are exported from Canada to other countries to purchase sweepstakes tickets. Indeed, apart from the moral question the export of Canadian dollars to other countries by this means is certainly a matter which should occupy the attention of the finance department of any government; there is no doubt about that whatsoever.
On the other side of the coin, if we permitted one province or two provinces to engage in this type of operation without general agreement that all are going to compete with each other in the field, we would be exporting dollars into those provinces from the nonparticipating provinces in Canada, which again would lead to difficulties.
It seems to me that the principle of this bill, which is to examine the whole question
2678	HOUSE OF
Administration of Justice of sweepstakes and lotteries and to find ways and means of obtaining from the Canadian people investment in such undertakings, with the reward of a higher return than might otherwise be obtained, is perfectly all right. On the other hand, before we begin to pass a bill of this kind I think we must examine the experience of other countries.
It is true that in the United States recently the state of New Hampshire passed this very controversial measure and set up a state lottery. It came into being amid a very stormy debate over the moral issue, with anxiety being expressed about possible reaction from neighbouring states and from the federal government-in some respects similar to the situation I attempted to describe a minute ago. The proceeds of this undertaking were to be used for school needs.
I think that one scheme which exploits, and for good, the desire of people to have a chance to make some extra money is that represented by the British system of lottery bonds. I think this scheme should certainly be examined by the Canadian government most carefully because it seems to me to have a great deal of merit. For example, in Great Britain bonds can be purchased, up to maximum blocks, of course. The investors do not receive any interest; instead, drawings are made and something equivalent to 4 per cent interest on the total amount of bonds sold over a specified period is distributed in the way of prizes.
