speechtext: Has the committee completed consideration of paragraph 12?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to paragraph 12 very briefly. I think
Income Tax Act
many of the initial remarks made by the Minister of Finance during his budget address in relation to the changes he proposes to bring about in the withholding tax were most plausible but, without adopting any holier than thou attitude, I think most of us recognize that if the minister had consulted his departmental officials over a year ago with regard to the proposals he introduced in his first budget he would not have found it necessary to propose the amendment in paragraph 12 that confronts hon. members at the present time. In fact, I feel that the approach of the minister and the government to the problem of the withholding tax has initially been a negative one.
While hon. members of all parties in the house recognize that the Canadian people and the Canadian economy are faced with a real problem, in that many of our secondary and primary industries are controlled by forces outside of the country, and are familiar with the problem in its basic form, I think we in Canada also recognize that at this time we need outside capital to develop our country. If we were able to go back to 1867 and live our economic lives over again I am not so sure we would not profit from some of the experiences we have had, but the objective economic facts are that at this time in 1964 we need capital from outside to develop our resources.
I am not one of those who want to hang the blame on the minister all the time, but certainly the fact is that the approach of the minister and the government to the problem of the withholding tax has been a negative one which has been damaging to Canada from the point of view of dealing with the problem of outside control of our resources. Indeed, it has been most damaging for Canada when we consider that we must have foreign capital to develop our resources.
I should like to state most emphatically that I hope the minister and the government will take a positive attitude from now on in relation to the problem of investment in and control of the economic resources of Canada. I hope that as soon as possible the government will implement those recommendations in the report of the royal commission on banking and finance which will encourage more Canadians and Canadian institutions to invest in both primary and secondary industries within Canada's economy.
I am not going to take the time of the committee by putting forward too much data, but I have always been one of those who have felt that far too many Canadians are keeping their money in a sock. This being so, rather than penalizing investors from outside of Canada who want to invest in our future because they really believe that Canada has

Income Tax Act
a bright economic future, I believe it is the responsibility of the minister in particular and the government in general not to engage in tinkering and wasting the time of the house and the country by experimenting-I am sure the minister would be the first to admit that the experiment has been an unhappy one-but rather to devote their thinking to implementing those measures which will encourage Canadians and Canadian institutions to invest in Canadian enterprises.
I should simply like to say that I do not believe the government alone can do this, but rather the government in co-operation with our stock exchanges and stock commissions will have to devise ways and means of encouraging not only those people in the high income brackets to invest in the Canadian economy but also those Canadians in the population generally who I believe have savings that can be devoted to this end. Again I repeat the proposition that I think far too many of our people, because of hidebound tradition, are keeping their money in a great big sock, and I think it is time that the minister and the government took positive measures to do something about this situation. These positive measures should be measures of the government's choice, and the positive measures that are to be found in the report of the royal commission on banking and finance, such as permitting broader scope for the investment of moneys to be found in pension funds and the like.
I do not know how much time it is going to take for the government to do these things but I think there is an immediate need for the government to do some serious thinking about policing stock transactions and the introduction of rules and regulations such as the rules and regulations of the securities and exchange commission in the United States. In sum and substance I am simply attempting to urge the minister to get away from the negative attitude which seems to have characterized the government in relation to its tinkering with the withholding tax and to adopt a positive attitude. I am sure that the opposition, realizing that this problem is much more important than party considerations, will support any government that forgets past activities and lets foreign investors know that their capital is welcome in Canada. I know we are living in difficult times and both the government of the day and the former government may have made particular and general mistakes which unfortunately may have had the result of discouraging foreign investors from coming into Canada.
Let us all regard this as a bipartisan proposition. Let the people outside of Canada
[Mr. Grafftey.f
know that their capital is welcome in Canada and that we need it. Let the minister and the government-I repeat this because it is something that needs repeating time and time again-try to encourage Canadians to take this money out of the sock and invest it in good Canadian securities.

If we may continue in that very reasonable vein the hon. member just started in this discussion, I wonder if we can get down to some very basic facts? The first one is that we have been in the habit of legislating for angels only to find that mortals inhabit this earth. We seem to be greatly shocked and surprised when we find that people behave like human beings. We have known for some time that more and more Canadian industry, Canadian mining and power are held by foreign investors. This is a situation which we realize now and for which we want an instant solution. Of course, there is no instant solution.
We talk about investment, but just what is the purpose of paragraph 12? I believe we are trying to repatriate the investment in Canadian companies. What we are really talking about is an element of risk. What we are saying is, if you put a little money into a new venture, 20 per cent of the people will lose and 80 per cent will make a fantastic amount. We know that in years gone by billions of dollars in profit have gone to people in the United States or Europe. We do not have this money. We must recognize that this is a gamble and that we are asking Canadians to invest.
If we may generalize for a moment we may say that the Canadian is very kind, considerate, and brave. He is a person who will never hurt your feelings. As hon. gentlemen here know, it is very difficult to find anyone who will admit a political affiliation because he may hurt your feelings. We are considerate and kind people, but we are also very apprehensive. We do not gamble. We are, therefore, going to require some incentive if we are going to gamble.
The second point I wish to mention is that the hon. member who has resumed his seat said Canadians have a lot of money. We do have a lot of money. I believe the minister will acknowledge that there is somewhere in the vicinity of $14 billion in savings in this country. We do not know how much money is hidden away in the socks of the Canadian people. If we can judge from the reports of the Brockville robbery, the safety deposit boxes of this country probably contain another $10 billion which is not being used. Possibly we have more in savings in this country for every man, woman and child than anywhere else. However, this is not the kind of money you gamble. This is money which

you scrimped to save and which was difficult to acquire. You do not play the market or gamble with this money. Most businessmen will acknowledge that the money with which people gamble or invest is the easy money, that is the money returned in the form of dividends or profits which people did not expect or which amounted to more than they expected. This is the kind of money that has not remained in this country.
I believe the minister has acknowledged the problem and tried to approach it in a reasonable way. We will have to provide an incentive if we are to find a solution to this problem. We have to consider that the Canadian is apprehensive. We will find it will be a great help in this problem when the Canadian is satisfied he will not starve in his old age. It will be a help when he realizes he has a good pension plan, good medical care and a good unemployment insurance scheme. This will remove that fear of what is going to happen in his old age. Even then, we are not going to get a bunch of Canadian investors.
I dare say you could have the stock market floor covered with shares and even then Canadians are not going to pick them up. We are not shares buyers. A program of education will have to be introduced, therefore, to let Canadians know what we are talking about when we urge them to invest in equity shares. We have to clean up the stock market. I think the minister will acknowledge, as will most members who have had any business dealings, that about 40 per cent of the equity money collected by a company is used in promotional sales. In so far as mining companies are concerned, this may amount to 80 per cent or 90 per cent. We cannot afford these promotional costs. There should be legislation governing this, perhaps by having all companies public companies, or some other method of controlling promotional sales.
I doubt if even this will induce Canadians to invest in shares because Canadians like the kind of risk that is 100 per cent sure. It is a curious thing that when we want Canadians to invest in equity shares we pass legislation which helps the Canadians put all their money in bricks and mortar. I am referring to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We do have legislation which invites Canadians to put money in mortgages. Surely, if our problem is connected with the share structure of companies, our real problem is specifically who is entitled to the dividends? We want the dividend money to stay here so it will be reinvested. So far as control of the company is concerned, that makes very little difference. Business is in business to make money, and will invest money in the manner that is most profitable to business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I might say a word or two about paragraph 12, this paragraph proposes that the 20 per cent rate of withholding tax on dividends paid after December 31, 1964, by a company that does

Income Tax Act
not have a degree of Canadian ownership, be reduced to 15 per cent. This will leave a rate of 15 per cent on dividends paid by companies that do not have a degree of Canadian ownership, and a rate of 10 per cent on Canadian companies that have a degree of Canadian ownership.
The purpose of subclause (a) is that the special tax of 5 per cent on increased dividends paid in the period between June 13, 1963 and January 1, 1965, by a company that does not have a degree of Canadian ownership, be repealed. This special tax was necessary to cover increased dividends paid before 1965 in anticipation of the 20 per cent rate scheduled to become payable on dividends after 1964. If there is not to be a rate of 20 per cent of dividends, this special tax is not necessary. We propose to repeal this tax with effect from the date of its enactment in 1963.
Consequential amendment (b) proposes that the increase from 15 per cent to 20 per cent in the tax on branch profits in Canada of non-resident companies shall not come into effect. The 1963 legislation provided for such an increase in tax after 1964, so that the tax on branches in Canada of non-resident companies would conform with the rate on dividends paid by companies that have not a degree of Canadian ownership.
Consequential amendment (c) proposes that the increase from 15 per cent to 20 per cent in the rate of tax on non-resident owned investment corporations, scheduled for 1964, shall not come into effect. If the rate of tax paid by companies without a degree of Canadian ownership had been increased to 20 per cent, it would have been necessary to impose the same rate of tax on the special kind of companies known as non-resident owned investment companies.
I presume from the tenor of the remarks so far that these changes will command the respect and the acceptance of all hon. members of the committee.

I can assure the Minister of Finance that these amendments will command the respect, attention and approbation of the official opposition because we have been urging them for the last year and we are very glad to see the minister is bringing them in now. I must say that I agree very much with what the hon. member for York East had to say in his comments about penalties themselves not being sufficient to accomplish the ends the minister has in mind.
Whatever we may think of the desirability, from the philosophical point, of the idea he has, as the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi said a few moments ago if we were starting out to negotiate confederation all over again, and if the minister happened to be 
minister of finance, we could have accomplished something that we may have missed in the intervening years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wasn't there then.

If the minister were there then we would not have the pleasure of having him here in front of us now. We are very glad he was not there because- and of course I would not say this myself- if he did not do better then than he did in his first budget, we would not have a Canadian parliament here at this time.
I am not going to repeat what has been said before. I think the best object lesson we have had was the speech given the other day by Mr. Ball, the United States under secretary of state. I suggested to the minister a year ago that in my opinion it was obviously necessary-and this the minister admitted-to get a treaty through the United States senate, to renegotiate a treaty if we were going to accomplish what he had in mind; and with the pressure on the United States senate, an election year being in the offing, and with the important legislation it had in front of it, it would be impossible for that body to renegotiate a treaty this year.
When you get the state under secretary in the United States making a speech such as he did on Saturday, attacking this policy hip and thigh, in shall we say polite but stern terms-I have forgotten how the minister described it-you can imagine what hope there would be of the United States senate passing such legislation this year.
The minister has said that the tax reductions in the United States have enabled him to retreat from the position he took when he brought this measure in a year ago. He is fortunate to have some justification for his retreat, but I do not think that is at all the material one. The material one is that he could not have got the legislation through and, if there had not been a tax treaty renegotiated, we would have been faced with a 30 per cent withholding tax on Canadian corporations in the United States, and this would be an absolutely impossible situation.
It is a very good thing that the minister has withdrawn from that position and that we are going back to the 15 per cent. The club has been withdrawn and there is now this small carrot held out. There should be more carrots. There should be a more positive approach. Obviously the banking commission, which reported the other day, felt that way, and there have been various briefs presented to it by the bankers' associations, making recommendations to deal with estate tax and other matters by which this end could be accomplished. We are well away from this legislation on which we embarked,

and from the clubs inherent in it in dealing with investment from outside.
There has been a great deal of controversy as to how much the investment of funds has dried up in this country. I know there are various aspects to that. I know the equalization tax in the United States played an important part, as well as the minister's first budget. I am not sure how far he can go in trying to delimit which had the greater effect, but I hope when the bill is before the house that he will be able to give us more information on that score. As it is, I am simply saying that we of the opposition appreciate the fact that this legislation is being amended, and this move certainly has our full hearted support.

The minister has said that apparently the provisions of paragraph 12 commend themselves to the committee. Lest silence appear to give consent, I want to express very briefly my point of view on this paragraph. Last year when the minister presented his budget he very properly expressed great concern about the growing control of the Canadian economy by foreign investors and he proposed some measures to rectify this situation. I do not think the measures he proposed at that time were very far reaching or likely to be effective, but at least they were a timid move in the right direction. I wish to express my regret that the minister has now completely retreated from the position he took last year and that he has not so far suggested any positive means of coping with the serious problem of the extensive control of the Canadian economy by foreign investors, particularly by the tremendous United States corporations.
I think it goes much further than this question of the withholding tax. When one finds under secretary George W. Ball, in the speech he made at Harrington, New York, warning the Canadian government that a very dim view will be taken of measures designed to make a change in the character of investment from equity to debt, it seems to me a serious point has been reached. If we are to get out of the dilemma in which we find ourselves there must, in my view, be a gradual change from equity control to loan capital and if Mr. Ball's words imply a warning to the Canadian government that any attempt to transfer indebtedness from an equity position to a loan capital position means there will be restrictions or retaliations, then, indeed, we have become an economic satellite and not a nation at all. While I do not intend to fight for the retention of these trifling provisions which are designed to move some of the indebtedness from an equity position to a debt position, I think this is symptomatic of the fact that the Canadian government is now in
Income Tax Act
retreat as far as any serious attempt to grapple with the problem of foreign control is concerned.
If the minister were simply removing these minor provisions in order to introduce some constructive and dynamic program, I would agree these would be no loss. But I see no signs of any such proposal. We in this party have a number of proposals which we have put forward from time to time and which I should like to make again. However, I am sure Your Honour would not permit me to discuss them under this paragraph and I therefore do not intend to seek to do so. But I think I should say to the minister that we are disappointed the government has apparently completely capitulated on this question of attempting to deal with foreign control of our economy; and in the absence of any proposals in the minister's budget speech and in the absence of any announced legislation, we can only assume that the government is giving up the battle after a very small and feeble effort.

Some brief references have been made to the royal commission on banking, and the previous speaker for the opposition observed that perhaps now was not the time to look back; that we should look ahead and recognize mistakes. The royal commission report made it clear that in its judgment there may have been mistakes on the part of the present administration as well as past administrations, and I think it might help us if we were to remember that the royal commission declared that it rejected the use of direct controls on international capital flows as disrupting to the efficient working of economic incentives and as having harmful long term effects. Then the report went on:
The country will no doubt continue to draw in resources from abroad at some times but on balance the economy need not be a large net user of foreign funds if soundly managed at home.
In this connection, the report points out that much of the capital inflow from 1958 to 1961 stemmed from inappropriate domestic credit policies.
Perhaps I might turn now to the observations made by the previous speaker. The leader of the New Democratic party spoke of the need for a challenging and positive program. Anybody who has been associated with the advanced training of young Canadians in commerce and law over the last two decades will readily recognize that there has been a tremendous improvement in management skills among Canadians during that period. Any legislation which draws attention to the fact that foreign investors may obtain important advantages by making use of these skills will prove worth while both to ourselves and to the companies concerned. If

Income Tax Act
those companies, in addition to taking advantage of Canadian skills, adjust their policies so as to be more in line with Canadian objectives, not only would their capital yield more, but the legislation under debate, instead of constituting a deterrent will constitute in my judgment both an incentive and an advantage.

Mr. Chairman, I am of the
opinion that this paragraph 12 will change the present situation very little and will not contribute anything towards creating a single new industry in Canada.
In this regard, I completely support the remarks made by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) to the effect that it is urgent for the government to take positive action and to make a forceful gesture in order to favour an economy controlled by Canadians.
In paragraph 12, we read the following:
That the 20 per cent rate of tax payable by a non-resident person... be reduced to 15 per cent, and that in consequence thereof:
(a) Part IID of the act imposing a tax equal to 5 per cent of certain dividends paid by a corporation that does not have a degree of Canadian ownership be repealed;
On the one hand, the 5 per cent exemption is reduced and, on the other, the 5 per cent tax now payable is removed. This means that we are running around in a circle with this paragraph 12, or this amendment to the Income Tax Act.
It was suggested a while ago that Canadians who have money or securities hidden away in wool stockings, etc., should be encouraged to take a gamble in order to help our secondary industries. We agree. However, it is not with the money hidden away nowadays in wool stockings that new secondary industries will be set up in Canada. Government action is absolutely necessary. The government must take its responsibilities. To suggest such solutions will not prevent Americans from continuing their control of the whole economy of the country. The government must assume its responsibilities, not in the face of the American people or the other peoples of the world, but in the face of Canadians themselves who are ready to work for the development of the natural resources of their country.
To that end, the government's co-operation is imperative. We have the necessary physical means in Canada, we have the talents, we have the brains, we have everything that is necessary to develop our natural resources and to turn them to the advantage of the whole population. The only element we do not have is credit, to finance the launching of an economic development program. The

Minister of Finance does not make such a suggestion. He forgets his responsibilities in that respect. He tries to make the Canadian people believe that a 5 per cent tax increase, levied on American companies will prevent Americans from continuing to exercise their control in Canada; but this will not allow Canadians to control their own economy.
Mr. Chairman, that clause was discussed earlier this afternoon and we have not made much progress. We are at a standstill. The Minister of Finance will not change his opinion or his attitude. Nevertheless, he should know that only concrete action will enable us to establish in our country an economic balance, the majority of which would be controlled by our fellow citizens. Then, secondary industries will pop up all over the country.
Some of our citizens have inventions to offer, things to present to the country which could be useful to the general welfare of our people.
The government listens but with half an ear.
It seems to me that we must regain our sense of responsibility; we must get back within the bounds of logic and common sense; we must stop erecting or spreading smoke screens before the public eye on the pretence that the government is helping greatly the Canadian people by imposing a 5 per cent tax on American companies operating businesses in Canada. In my opinion, it is to laugh in our people's face, to consider them as ignorant people who know nothing of what is happening in their country and who believe that the Minister of Finance actually is assisting them in gratifying a little less the American people, while still leaving to them the control of our Canadian economy, as they have it at the present time.
If we want to keep and help our Canadian industries, the Minister of Finance only has to ask the industrial expansion bank to provide an amount of credit proportionate to our physical capability of setting up secondary industries which, in turn, will create jobs and increase our national production. Then, it would no longer be necessary to deal with odd questions like the one covered by paragraph 12 of this amendment to the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this paragraph proposes that where a partner sells his interest, the appropriate part of the amount he receives as the selling price shall be deemed to be received on account of the disposition of depreciable property. This will make it possible to recapture depreciation which the partners claimed in recent years, or to allow a terminal loss in respect of the depreciable property, depending upon the circumstances.
It is just as if a corporation sells some depreciable assets at a profit. The amount of capital cost allowance that it has claimed in earlier years is recouped by the crown as a charge against the corporation's profits, and this provision is intended to apply the same principle when a partner retires.

On paragraph 14, Mr. Chairman, I think there is raised a question which the minister should explain carefully to the committee at this time. This is the paragraph which provides that family allowances will be paid in respect of children who otherwise would not be qualified; that is, children over the age of 16. The parents of such children will receive for this year a deduction of $470. Ordinarily, if they were dependants and not in receipt of family allowance, they would receive a deduction from income of $550. If they were in receipt of family allowance for the year, they would only receive a deduction of $300, I think.
In this case I think the minister is splitting the difference, shall we say, and assuming that the legislation will not come into effect until some time this year, possibly not until next fall; therefore they will receive $470 and then, presumably, the family allowance for the balance of the year. That raises the question of the payment of family allowances under this paragraph and the deductibility therefrom. The whole field has yet to be dealt with, I quite appreciate that; but this is a situation which should be clarified now as far as the minister is concerned.
As I understand it from newspaper reports and, I think, from the statement of the Prime Minister as well, and possibly from the statement of the Minister of Finance-I am not sure about that-the situation is as follows. The Prime Minister spoke on this when dealing with the arrangements that were made between the province of Quebec and the government of Canada and said that the province of Quebec had, of course, been paying for some years an educational grant to children over the family allowance age. I think the province certainly deserves a great deal
Income Tax Act
of commendation for so doing. It has been an educational grant for those who stayed in school and has been paid out of provincial revenues. Now we are going to pay family allowance in respect of all children who remain in school over the ages of 16 and 17. But in the province of Quebec, this being an educational grant, as I gather from what the Prime Minister said the other day, the province will continue to make that payment in respect of the children and there will be an abatement from the federal treasury to the province of the amount, roughly, that has been paid to the parents of the children in Quebec. In Ontario and the rest of Canada the family allowance will be paid.
It may be-and this is a situation which I think the minister should clarify now- that a parent living on the other side of the river here with one dependant 16 years of age will be receiving $10 a month from the province of Quebec in respect of this educational grant and at the same time will be receiving the deduction in so far as the dependant is concerned, because he will not be receiving family allowance. On the other hand, with regard to the parent living on this side of the river and receiving a family allowance, the dependancy will only result in a deduction of $300 a year instead of $550. That is an anomalous situation which has caused some discussion in the press and elsewhere in Canada. Therefore I think that with regard to this paragraph the minister should clarify the situation as it will be when the legislation is completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this particular paragraph of the resolution, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings pointed out, deals only with the difference between the $550 that is normally allowed for a dependant and the $300 that is allowed for a dependant in respect of whom family allowance is being paid to the parents for a period. The difference between those two amounts is $250. It is expected that these payments will apply for the months of September to December, inclusive, this year-that is to say, four months-and a third of $250 is roughly $80. This explains why the figure is $470.
In the application of this new proposal to the province of Quebec certain difficulties arose. As the hon. member pointed out, the province of Quebec has been paying an educational grant for some years. This went back either to 1960, or it began in 1961. In the case of the province of Quebec the amounts are paid to the children, or in the right of the children, rather than to the parents. Because of this, and because I suppose it was a payment by a provincial government, there has been no change in the

Income Tax Act
income tax deductions allowable to the parents. They are not reduced because the payments are made, as I say, to the children.
I would remind the members of this committee that under the Quebec plan this educational grant applies for ten months only, not for 12, so the payment in respect of a 16 or 17 year old child to continue at school amounts to $100 a year. Under the proposed federal plan which will be presented to the house as soon as the legislation has been drafted the amount will be $10 a month and will apply for 12 months, and it will be paid, as are the family allowances, to the parents. I suppose that theoretically the federal plan could apply to everyone in Canada, but in that case the additional $10 per month per child in the case of Quebec would be superimposed upon an existing plan under which the province is already paying $10 per month by way of educational grants. I think most people would agree that although it would be nice for the people of Quebec to get it twice, it would not be a reasonable thing to do.
The government of the province of Quebec has pointed out that they have a plan which has been in existence for three or four years. It has been well accepted. It meets their requirements and understandably they do not wish to change it. On the other hand, in extending the principle of family allowances the federal government certainly would not wish to pay something which could be interpreted as an educational grant. After all, there are certain sensitivities in these matters as well as certain constitutional rights and responsibilities, and I not think that the members of this committee would agree that this would be a wise course for the federal government to embark upon. And, of course, the federal government has no intention of doing so.
Therefore, the problem has been to find a workable and reasonable compromise. It is proposed-and I am now answering my hon. friend's question, although this will doubtless be discussed again when the legislation is before the house-that an amount be paid to the province of Quebec which will be calculated at the net amount which would have been paid in respect of children remaining at school in the province of Quebec, less the reduction in the allowances in the rest of the country in the case of parents in the higher income brackets. This deduction is quite substantial and this is the proposal which will be presented to the house when this legislation is ready for consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I would not want to let this occasion go by without [Mr. Nowlan.J	,
rectifying one statement made by the minister. In his remarks he said that allowances were paid to the children, which is not the case. In fact, they are paid directly to the mother of the child.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I just correct that. They are paid in the right of the children; but the children are a little young so probably the money goes to the mother.

Only a few short remarks, Mr. Chairman.
When Mr. Lesage was a federal minister, he never considered as an interference by the federal government in the field of education the fact that this government paid family allowances to children of a certain age and to those who are still studying. That is why I am surprised that Mr. Lesage objects to the decision of the federal government to grant a further amount and extend the period during which family allowances are paid.
I understand that the Quebec government pays family allowances to children at a more advanced age than the federal government but, in my opinion, the basic reason why Mr. Lesage objects to an extension of those family allowances by the federal government, is not so much because provincial autonomy is jeopardized, but because the provincial government is already paying a school allowance, and Mr. Lesage prefers to get those sums of money back and use them for other purposes.
Consequently, I believe that it would be more normal for Mr. Lesage to receive those sums of money and to give them to children who continue their studies.
That is my personal opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I might just clear up any misunderstanding on this last point. As I said earlier, there was some discussion as to whether the very fortunate children-or perhaps the very fortunate mothers-of the province of Quebec should get two $10 per month payments, one from the province and one from the federal government.
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, that is a very natural comment and I can quite understand it. I dare say that that is a comment which would be made by many of the mothers in the province of Quebec. However, I would remind my hon. friend that payments are made to the mothers and not to the fathers. The fact is that there are those who feel there are a lot of demands which are made upon the relatively meagre resources of governments, both federal and provincial, and that this problem having been looked after in the

province of Quebec in 1960 or 1961 it would not make sense to duplicate it. It was for that reason and because their plan has been in existence for some time and is working well-and no one wants to abandon a plan which has been successful-that it is proposed to handle the matter in the way I have described.

Mr. Chairman, what I meant is that Mr. Lesage reminds me of a magician.
The federal government wants to pass that legislation, vote those sums of money which in the other provinces, will normally be going to the children attending school, whereas Mr. Lesage will get that money and will be able to do what he pleases with it. In other words, the money he will receive from the federal government will not go to the children of Quebec still attending school. He will be able to do what he pleases with it.
Everyone knows that Mr. Lesage once was a cabinet minister in Ottawa and that he is now premier of Quebec. I feel that his attitude has changed completely; he is not the same man, in short, he does not have the same political conscience. That is what I wanted to draw to the attention of the house.
I understand why Mr. Lesage so rightly objects to the federal government's intrusion in the field of education, but whatever means the latter might have taken to satisfy the Quebec premier, I would have wished that, upon receipt of that money, Mr. Lesage would have been compelled to distribute it to children who still attend school, even if the provincial government already provides a certain amount in that connection. In fact, I feel such a course of action would have been more normal.

Mr. Chairman, I must admit that I did not follow the minister's explanation too clearly and I would ask him to explain the matter in a little more detail. Will the exemption that parents of children 16 and 17 in the nine provinces can claim be reduced to $300 and will the parents of children of the same age in Quebec continue to get an exemption of $550? Would the minister take a family just across the river, let us say, with one child going to school and a similar family in Ontario, compare the two and explain the matter so that we may follow it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a difference now between a family in Quebec and a family in Ontario which I will explain in a moment. That difference will be narrowed. At the moment a family in Quebec receives $550 in respect of or on behalf of-I forget the
Income Tax Act
legal phrase-a child who continues in school up to the age of 18. I am informed that the age is higher than that. This is something that the people of the province of Quebec get from their provincial government, and that the people of no other province receive. Therefore parents in the province of Quebec now have a decided advantage in this respect over people in the other nine provinces. That is the way it is now.
Under the proposed plan the present arrangement in the province of Quebec will, as far as I know, continue without change. That is the intention of the government of Quebec. In all the other provinces, however, the federal government will extend the present family allowances at the rate of $10 per month for 12 months, whereas in Quebec it is only 10 months, and apply exactly the same formula that now applies up to the age of 15 in so far as allowances are concerned.
Therefore if you take somebody on one side of the river and compare her with somebody on the other side of the river I think you will be able to show that there is a difference in the net amount they will receive and that difference will be reduced in the future. Because the Quebec plan was introduced some time ago, because it is an established plan and because, understandably, I think, the government there feels it would be unacceptable to change it, the net amount after the deduction of the statutory allowances for children that would have been payable in the province of Quebec to mothers in the province of Quebec under the federal scheme will be paid to the government of that province. I do not know whether I should comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Assomption-Montcalm.

All I am trying to find out is whether this is an equitable arrangement.

Income Tax Act
Do I understand what the minister is now telling us is something like this? In the province of Quebec the provincial government will continue to pay $100 a year per child. I am putting it on an annual basis. In other parts of Canada the federal government will pay to each family $120 per year for 16 and 17 year-olds. Will the financial equivalent which is to be paid to the province of Quebec be on the basis of $100 per child or on the basis of $120 per child. My second question is: Do I understand that the exemption for parents in Quebec will continue to be $550 whereas in the rest of Canada it will be reduced to $300? Will the minister answer those questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but in calculating the financial equivalent to be paid to the province of Quebec it will be worked out at $120 less the difference between the allowances of $550 and $300, which makes quite a difference in the total tax paid by any individual. Therefore it will not be the gross amount of $120. Let me take my hon. friend as an example, although as he is roughly my age perhaps I had better pick somebody younger. I do not know whether the hon. member has teenage children. If a member of this house has two teenage children his wife will receive-
In Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the rest of Canada-$240, but the amount of the deduction that the member can claim for those two children will only be $600 because his wife gets this extra amount instead of being $550 times two or a total of $1,100. So his tax will go up and the amount that the tax goes up is obviously an offset to the total that is paid. Exactly the same calculation will be made in arriving at the fiscal equivalent that is due to the province of Quebec. Therefore the province of Quebec, taking the province as representing all the people of Quebec, will be in exactly the same position as any other province.

May I clarify one point? I think I understand the minister now, but am I correct that parents in the province of Quebec will get $100 instead of $120, but they will save almost the equivalent amount on income tax, so it works out reasonably fairly? The province of Quebec will collect on the basis of $120 even though it is only paying $100, but there will be deducted from the fiscal equivalent paid to them the amount of income tax which the federal government would have collected if the exemption had been only $300 in Quebec instead of $550. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

May I ask the minister
at this stage, for the sake of consistency-* and that is apparently the approach-why did the government not adopt the Quebec formula or the Quebec plan? Then we would not be spending all evening on this thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that the members of the government spent many evenings in trying to arrive at the best solution of this very complicated problem.
Is this the best solution? I doubt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The government thinks it is. Perhaps the hon. member may think so too when I have finished my explanation.
If the government had proposed to this house or, when the time comes if it did propose to this house, that we just adopt the Quebec plan holus-bolus we would not be extending the family allowance procedure at all. We would be doing something different. The family allowance procedure has been in force, I think, for 20 years. There has been no question about it. No one, to my knowledge, has ever challenged its constitutionality. If we were to adopt an entirely new approach for people in the 16 and 17 year old brackets, then I would have to go to the Minister of Justice and ask him if he was quite sure this would be acceptable.
The intention has always been in connection with this legislation that it should represent an extension of the family allowance scheme to apply to people at 16 and 17 years, because times have changed in 20 years and people no longer leave school, or we hope they no longer leave school at 15. This was the purpose and the intention. Apart from that, the problem has been to find a fair, reasonable and equitable basis for compensating the government of Quebec who, understandably, do not want to withdraw or change their system which has been in effect for three or four years.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the remarks made by the Minister of Finance, but I feel he was ill informed by his adviser when he told the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) that school allowances were paid even after the age of 18 in the province of Quebec.
The granting of those school allowances ends at 18. But what I feel is unfair is that the Minister of Finance seems to consider as a dependant child one who attends an institution or a school, and that is the basis of his argument. Consequently, a 16 or 17 year old youth who does not attend school in Quebec would be deprived of the family allowance

from 16 to 18 years of age, while in the other provinces, such a child would get it.
Therefore, the word "dependant" should not be limited to those who go to school, because it may happen that a sick or crippled child remains dependant on his parents without going to school.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member? I am afraid that when I attempted to explain this I simplified it too greatly. I can assure my hon. friend this allowance will apply to children who are sick or invalids.

I thank the minister for clearing up that point, but here again it seems to me that the basic exemption will vary in the province of Quebec as compared to the other provinces. The minister stated that in Quebec the deductibility will reach a maximum of $470. But what about poor or large families? The individual who does not pay income tax for lack of sufficient income will not be able to benefit by this basic exemption of $470 and he will lose his monthly allowance of $20 compared to children of other provinces.
I believe the minister should, in the bill which he will submit to the house later, provide a special allowance based on 12 rather than ten months per year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, all I can say in reply to that is the people in Quebec will be treated in exactly the same way as they always have been. So far as the compensation that will be paid to Quebec is concerned, I can say with some assurance that I have every confidence in the government of Quebec being able to check the arithmetic very carefully.

I am wondering too, Mr. Chairman, about the grants that are going to be made to Quebec in lieu of this program. These family allowances are rigidly controlled by the Department of National Health and Welfare and in certain cases children would not be eligible under the program. For instance, a person over 16 not attending school would not qualify for the additional allowance. It seems to me the allowance regulations are going to differ between the federal family allowance scheme operative in all other provinces except Quebec, and the Quebec scheme. We are going to get serious discrepancies.
I can conceive of a situation whereby a mother in Quebec would receive the $100 a year allowance from the provincial authorities for income tax purposes and would be able to deduct the full $550 exemption for youngsters between 16 and 17, whereas a 20220-171
Income Tax Act
family in a province other than Quebec in the identical situation would not receive the extra family allowance and would still be allowed only the same deduction for income tax purposes. The question I have for the minister is, at the time these negotiations were being conducted did the federal government examine the kind of controls that were going to be imposed on this program to ensure there would not be a discrepancy here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps questions of this kind could be dealt with better when the legislation is before the house. I can assure my hon. friend that this problem has been gone into very thoroughly. I think it might perhaps becloud a very interesting and a very good discussion on this resolution if we get into a discussion of another piece of legislation that will be presented very shortly.

I understood the minister to say the exemption for parents in the nine provinces will be $300 and in Quebec it will be $550 for children aged 16 or 17 years going to school. Now, how do we know whether or not a child is at school? How is this arrived at? I think I understand the Ontario situation; is Quebec operated the same way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same tests will apply in the future as apply now, and family allowances are not paid now unless children go to school.
The question is, how do we know the child is at school? What controls have we?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is something I would prefer to discuss when the legislation is before the house. I do not know whether that will be next week or next month, but it will certainly have to be soon. I will be properly briefed then and I hope I will be in a position to answer my hon. friend's question. My understanding is that the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare have an inspection service, and they check up with the schools.
Maybe we can hold over paragraph 14 until we have this information that the minister speaks of.

On this clause

and at first glance one might think I was getting off the subject-I would like to point out that often, both in this chamber and outside it, I have proposed closer liaison between the federal government and the provincial governments. I proposed the establishment of a secretariat or other body for federal-provincial affairs,

Income Tax Act
and if any example demonstrates the necessity for such a body it is the debate in this committee tonight.
I am not blaming the minister for this. I know we are still a young country and are still evolving our procedures, but my proposal to this effect was talked out the other day during private members' hour. What is going on here tonight indicates the immediate need for the government to sit down with the provinces, not tomorrow but almost tonight. I have spoken about this to my colleagues, to my friends in the press gallery and to my friends on both sides of the chamber. There has been far too much postponement about it.
There is an immediate need for the establishment of more sophisticated bodies, call them secretariats or what you will. Tonight's debate indicates the type of misunderstandings and disagreements that can take place when we lack this liaison or these sophisticated bodies for federal-provincial affairs. I should think the minister would be getting pretty tired of having ultimatums issued to him by the premier of Quebec, but I congratulate the minister.
Every sincere Canadian, no matter what party he belongs to, is happy about the type of arrangement the minister and the government have been able to make with Quebec in the last few days. I congratulate the minister and the government upon it, and we are putting party after country when we say that.
However, I remember just before that the federal government was threatened by the premier of Quebec that this whole question was going to be brought immediately before the supreme court. Within the short space of one year we have had a Liberal premier telling a Liberal government at Ottawa that he is going to have his way, or else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The standing order is well known to the hon. member, which requires that discussion in committee be strictly relevant to the resolution before us, and I would ask him to keep that in mind.

I bow to that ruling, but I
would point out that before the arrangement was made with the province of Quebec, the premier of Quebec stated that this whole matter was going to be brought by his government before the supreme court, and I think that is relevant. That being the case I would like to ask the minister, before this arrangement was made with the province of Quebec, did any of the government's advisers advise it that this whole proposal was unconstitutional?
Before taking my seat I offer this idea in all sincerity to the committee, because I think 
it is a very appropriate time to do it. The debate taking place tonight, and what has happened outside the committee in relation to this whole problem, indicates that there is a pressing need for more sophisticated bodies to deal with liaison between the federal government and the provinces.

I have only a few words to say about paragraph 14.
I feel that the reference to exemptions which must not exceed $470 if an allowance is paid under the Family Allowances Act causes confusion more than anything else.
Many people think that the province of Quebec will benefit more than the other provinces and will get a preferential treatment under this paragraph 14.
I wonder whether the minister intends to introduce legislation in this field in the near future? The minister and the government should have granted a general increase in family allowances for children 17 and 18 years old, under the same conditions now applying to children getting allowances since 1945-if a child stops going to school, as the minister knows, the payment of those family allowances is stopped. It has always been so. Now, to avoid this confusion which exists at the present time between Quebec legislation and federal legislation which is interpreted in Quebec as a federal intrusion in a provincial field, why not increase family allowances now granted to other children?
If Quebec decides to pay school allowance in addition to family allowances, that would be its own business. If Ontario wants to do likewise that is also Ontario's own business and if that province does not want to do so, it does not have to. I think that it would justify the federal point of view, if we had standard legislation throughout Canada. It is useless to divide. There has not been any division in the case of family allowances since 1945.
All the provinces and all the mothers have accepted it, like the minister said a moment ago. But since the minister does not see any objection to the mothers of our children receiving an allowance $10 larger, why does he not introduce general legislation to continue family allowances up to 18 years of age. Then, let the province of Quebec administer its own educational system, and let Mr. Jean Lesage continue, I hope, to pay $10 a month to the children of the province of Quebec. And that will free the federal government.

I realize the minister is in a difficult position. He is trying to explain what,

prima facie, is a very simple question. Unfortunately for him it is complicated by the fact that the Prime Minister, in making his statement, indicated that instead of this family allowance being extended into the province of Quebec there would be an equivalent provided. Consequently, when we look at paragraph 14 we must look at it in the light of what the Prime Minister said in his announcement.
What the minister has been attempting to do is to indicate what type of regulations there will be in the future, so that in the view of the government there will be equity done between the parents of 16 and 17 year old children in Quebec and the parents of 16 and 17 year old children outside Quebec. This is how I understand his proposition. We must take these two statements together, and the fact that the government of Quebec has stated it wants this allowance in another form.
What puzzles me is how we can reconcile that with the fact that for 20 years family allowances have been paid into every province with a stipulation that if a child ceases to attend school the allowance ceases to be paid. I realize in making this comment the minister may be driven to consider what may be the type of legislation to be introduced in the future, but for the last 20 years family allowances have been paid under the provisions of the legislation which provides, under section 4, that the allowance ceases to be payable if the child does not regularly attend school as required by the laws of the province where he resides. I realize this is not the time when the minister can give a complete answer, but nevertheless we are being asked to approve paragraph 14, and we must keep this in mind. How do we reconcile this provision which has been in the Family Allowances Act for 20 years with the distinction which we are now asked to make with respect to the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that is a perfectly clear question and I will try to answer it. In the normal course I would have expected that if it were decided that family allowances should be continued in respect of children in school after the age of 15, that is while they are 16 and 17, there would just be an extension and we would go along in exactly the same way as before. That is what will happen, except in the province of Quebec. Why should there be a different formula for Quebec? The answer is that Quebec is already in this field. The province is already paying an educational grant to children who are 16 and 17 years of age.
Theoretically, I suppose, if the federal government wanted to extend the present family allowance arrangements up to the age of 18 they could do so and this would apply 20220-1714
Income Tax Act
everywhere in Canada, including Quebec; and the government of Quebec could in that event do one of two things: It could either continue to pay its present education grants, which would mean there would be roughly twice as much paid in the province of Quebec in respect to children aged 16 and 17 as would be paid elsewhere in Canada, or, alternatively, it could say: The federal government is now paying these sums; we shall stop our payments. Either of these decisions would be perfectly logical, I suggest. However, the government of the province of Quebec says: We have been in this field for three or four years; we are doing it in a way which seems to us reasonable; a way which seems acceptable to our people, one which is well established; and we want to go on doing it that way; we would prefer it if you would pay to us the equivalent of what would have been paid by the federal government net, after income tax and so on, and if it were paid directly in respect of the children.
Anyone could argue whether or not this was a good way of doing it. As I say, the federal government could charge right ahead, ignore the fact that this is an established program in Quebec and insist on paying the amounts directly to the mothers despite the fact that the government of the province does not want this done. Or the government of Canada could say: We recognize the fact that you have been in this field for three or four years. We are not going to pay any more than the citizens of Quebec would have got under our new scheme, but instead of paying them double and embarrassing everybody we shall pay the net equivalent to the government of Quebec. And this is what will be proposed when the legislation is presented in this house.

I believe this extended discussion would not have taken place if the minister had been able to say right at the outset that there would be no difference in the income tax deductions applicable to the mothers in the province of Quebec and those in the rest of Canada. He said there would be a financial equivalent but it would not be the same.
Is it fair to assume that the education grant being paid to the people in Quebec is possible because of the tax-sharing arrangement by the federal government-in other words, because there is an element of federal assistance in those payments? If so, it seems unfair that there should be this difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say the situation would be exactly the same, because it has not been exactly the same for the last three or four years. It has been very different.

Income Tax Act
Amounts paid by the province of Quebec in respect of children in that province have not had any effect on deductions. They have been treated as though they were made to the child, not to the mother.

My point is that if there is an element of federal assistance in the provincial scheme for paying education grants there must be some way of working this out so that for income tax purposes there would be no difference as between parents in Quebec and parents in other parts of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I appreciate the hon. member's suggestion and his feelings in the matter but I do not know of any way in which this could be done.

When I addressed a question to the minister earlier on the subject-admittedly it was not in such clear terms as were used by my hon. friend from Portage-Neepawa-the hon. gentleman suggested we should wait until the legislation was before the house, at which time, he said, it would be possible to go into the details of this program. I do not quarrel with that position, but I do not necessarily want details of this program. I want an assurance that the controls which have been placed on this program, be it administered in Quebec or in any other part of the country under the authority of the federal government, are going to be equally effective. Arrangements for deductions should be the same for all Canadians, especially if the programs are to be similar. Surely if we enter into this bargain with the people of Quebec-and it is a bargain for those who live in Quebec-Canadians who live in other provinces should not be subjected to rules and regulations, under the family allowances program, which people in Quebec will not be obliged to keep. If the minister can give me this assurance I shall be prepared to wait for the details on a later occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am perfectly prepared to give that assurance to the best of my knowledge and belief. If anything, I think the checking up process will be more complete in the province of Quebec than elsewhere in Canada. I do not wish to go into details but I think I am safe in assuring the hon. member that there is nothing to worry about on that score.

There seems to be a fundamental matter here which should be taken into consideration. As I understand the minister's explanation, the people of Quebec are to be treated differently from people in other parts of Canada. I think that is unfortunate. I know there is to be a compensatory payment made to the province of Quebec, but

I understand that the mothers in Quebec are to receive $10 for ten months of the year whereas parents in other parts of Canada are to receive $10 per month for 12 months of the year. I would have to put myself on record as favouring a program whereby all mothers across Canada would be treated alike-
Hear, hear.

*-and the children paid $10 for 12 months of the year. I think it is up to any provincial government to accommodate its arrangements in such a field as this to an over-all scheme, and in this I agree with the hon. member for Peace River. In effect we are simply extending family allowance at the rate of $10 per month from the age of 16 to the age of 18. That is what we are doing. Why not come right out and do it openly without any of these confusing arrangements which seem to enter into this question? Why not simply extend family allowances from age 16 to age 18 and have done with it? The present act takes care of school attendants and children who are dependant. The children who are ill or cannot attend school are taken care of. The children who are healthy and do not attend school come under the same regulations and the same conditions as do other children at the present time.
I feel we are on the wrong track. There is a fundamental point which this committee should take into consideration and I do not think we can pass it over as lightly as has been suggested. I think we should increase family allowances to the age of 18, leave it at that and let the different provinces deal with it as they will.

Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the hon. member who said a few words a while ago. I felt like him, but coming from the province of Quebec I thought I would give the opportunity to somebody else to speak for me, and I want to thank the member very warmly.
It seems to me, after taking into consideration everything we have heard tonight, that there is only one aim in the mind of the minister, and it is to save the face of his friend the premier of the province of Quebec. I think the mothers of the province of Quebec owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Middlesex West, and I would like the minister to take into consideration the recommendation he has just made, and forget the petty politics that seem to be underneath this matter and governing all the acts and movements of the minister. Please put us on the same level as everybody, and try to forget your friend the premier of the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, at the present time the government of the province of Quebec pays the children attending school $10 a month during a period of ten months, that is during the school year, whereas the federal government pays $10 a month during 12 months.
Under the circumstances, I am of the opinion that this situation discriminates against the mothers and children of Quebec.
I feel that if the federal government reached an agreement with the province of Quebec about that sum of $10, it would have been very important to make Mr. Lesage and his government pay that $10 during 12 months instead of ten, as they do in the other provinces where mothers will receive $10 during 12 months. That is discrimination against mothers and, consequently, I should like to know whether the minister intends to intervene with the Quebec premier to remedy the situation.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Is the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm aware of the fact that the Quebec premier has announced that his province will pay $10 a month over a 12 month period just the same as the federal government?
I will have a few words to say on that point later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank my hon. friend. I was just about to say that I am quite certain the premier of the province of Quebec will do right by the mothers of that province.

Mr. Chairman, I am not intervening in this debate, which is very interesting and, I hope, helpful, but I would just like to say a few words. This is a very involved and complicated matter that we have been discussing tonight. Therefore I think it is desirable that we should read the record and the explanations the minister has given so we may obtain a proper understanding of exactly what has been done. It is rather difficult during the course of debate to follow this matter in the detail that I think is required.
We are now told that the payments are exactly the same in all provinces, and that at least is one step on the road to uniformity. There is still the problem of the income tax deductions under the Income Tax Act, and I think this is perhaps more serious than the minister was inclined to recognize or admit when he referred to it a short while ago. Previously there was a lesser payment made to
Income Tax Act
the province of Quebec; now it is a larger one. With regard to the deduction which the minister mentioned, if you get a deduction of $300 a year for a dependancy in one case, and $550 in another case, it depends entirely on the taxable income as to how much deduction that may be worth. There is no point at all in saying it is equalized because of this, that and the other. We can all imagine a good many cases where a deduction of $550 would be infinitely more valuable than the compensating factors which the minister mentioned. I think we have to study this question. As I said, we will have the bill before us, I presume, in the reasonably near future and we will be able to discuss it then in all its details.
I want to impress upon the minister that we want-this has been said on this side of the chamber

absolute equality, and no one wants there to be any interference whatsoever with the Quebec scheme. As the minister said, they started their scheme some time ago, no one wants to interfere with it and no one wants to impose a tax on it, because we realize the constitutional complications that would arise immediately if you had an educational grant there and it was treated in a different way than we would have to treat it in regard to the other provinces. But I think we have to go some way yet in order to achieve uniformity among provinces in this matter. That is highly desirable, of course. We cannot have a family on one side of the river here treated in one way, and a family on the other side of the river treated in a different way.
Hear, hear.

That certainly would not be co-operative federalism; it would be the disruption of federalism, the disruption of federation, and we do not want to see that happen. As far as I am concerned-and I think most of us are concerned about this-there has been a fairly long discussion on this matter and I believe the minister appreciates the viewpoint that has been put forward. I can imagine that he has discussed this matter at length on various occasions and in a far different place from this, and has heard every argument which has been advanced tonight- and possibly he has raised some of them himself.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 15.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister whether under this paragraph students who go to trade school, business college, or even take an apprenticeship in a factory where they are learning a trade or receiving technical training, qualify for this allowance.

For the sake of those who may read Hansard, may I say that I am looking at a text in form roughly the size of Hansard, and this simple little definition of Canadian ownership starts half way down page 6, runs all the way down page 7, runs all the way down page 8, and runs almost to the end of page 9. speechtext: The first question is from the hon. member for Lambton West.

maintopic: SHIPPING-REPORTED U.S. ACTION TO CONTROL LAKE HURON WATER LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I asked the Minister of Transport a question this afternoon was because the harbours along the shores of lake Huron are becoming useless. This year I
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion understand the drop in the level of water has reached the point where the water level is approximately three feet below average. My riding, like others in the lake Huron area, is suffering a great deal because of this. For example, Grand Bend has a number of fishing companies which produced about $750,000 five years ago, quite a large amount for a small area. This is now reduced to about $500,000 per year. The harbour has been dredged each year, but if the harbour has no water all the dredging that can be done is not going to help the fishing boats in and out of the harbour. What they need is water.
Following along the lake Huron shore of my riding I come to Port Franks, Perch creek and Point Edward where there is a great deal of commercial fishing which is very important to these areas. Business that requires river dockage suffers at the port of Sarnia. I believe the port of Sarnia is classified as part of the seaway and if the water levels of the lake continue to go down that very busy port of Sarnia will be in real trouble unless something is done. This is the reason I asked the Minister of Transport this question this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: SHIPPING-REPORTED U.S. ACTION TO CONTROL LAKE HURON WATER LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the hon. member for Lambton West has to do with a matter that was decided in principle some years ago. According to the information available to me, at the time the dredging was started in the St. Clair river-I recall the very beginnings of that because I was minister of citizenship and immigration at the time and it affected the Indian reserve on Walpole island-the United States government also proposed that they should make a study of the possibility of putting some kind of barrier in the river just below the Blue Water bridge in order to maintain the levels as much as could be done in that way without interference with navigation, and to offset any possible effect that dredging might have.
However, this was not the kind of thing that could be done very effectively without a good deal of model testing and experimentation. The government of Canada agreed in principle to having this matter considered. The information I have is that agreement was given in 1962 by the previous administration, and I think very wisely, and that this experimentation is now going on. I sincerely hope, as I am sure all hon. members do, that it may be successful and that some definitive action may be taken as the result of it.
I am afraid, however, that however valuable this may be as a long term measure it is not going to have very much effect, and in fact cannot possibly have any effect at all, in the present season. We are faced with a very grave problem indeed not only in lake

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Descha-telets) and I and our officials have been considering this matter and we are going to do anything we can to alleviate the situation by dredging. But the water just is not there. This is something that I am afraid can only be cured by more water.
