speechtext:
I have a somewhat similar question to that of the hon. member who just spoke. The low water levels on the great lakes and the Georgian bay have been causing concern for about a year now. In 1963 it was generally felt that the problem was one of a natural cycle. It was so explained to those of us who made inquiries and it was said that it would soon right itself.
However, when the ice went out in 1964 it became obvious that this was not just a low cycle. There was no restoration of the water level and, at the moment, it is not just a problem for many places along the lakes: It is a disaster. I saw pictures published in the Parry Sound North Star and in the Globe and Mail this morning which indicate how disastrous this situation is.
As the minister has just stated, members representing constituencies, particularly along Georgian bay and lake Huron, have been very concerned. The government, if I may be fair,
I believe has accepted the advice it received that this was a cycle and there was not much that could be done about it. While this is undoubtedly a factor, and while undoubtedly there is low precipitation, many of us fear that underlying this may be something more fundamental, that there may be not just a short term problem but a major one such as the drainage away of water.
In asking the numerous questions that have been asked, we are not trying to attach 

blame. We are merely attempting to get the government to undertake some active measures to have the situation rectified. Several indicators show that the lack of precipitation is not the whole answer. Over the week end, I verified this. For example, the Muskoka lakes and most of the smaller inland lakes have normal water levels now. Lake Nipis-sing, according to an answer I received yesterday, has water one foot higher than it was last year or the year before. We are not suggesting that any of these lakes should be lowered because that would merely be extending the problem into other lakes.
We do feel that the studies that are being undertaken by the United States corps of engineers now indicate there is a problem to be met. We are hoping that some long term measures will be seriously considered so that we will not find the situation is a permanent one. My question is really to determine whether the government has now been persuaded that some action is necessary and that some research will have to be done. If the Minister of Transport would make a statement along those lines, then I am sure we would all like to hear that statement.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: EXPERIMENTS BY U.S. CORPS OP ENGINEERS
speechtext:
I could not agree more with what the hon. gentleman has just said. I do not pose as an expert, myself, but I do not believe, although there has been a serious lack of precipitation in the last two or three years, that is the whole answer to the problem. I did not bring the figures with me, but I have been looking at them. It is quite apparent that there has been, over two or three years, a lack of precipitation. There may be something cyclical about these things. However, it is a little questionable whether our records extend back in a really accurate way long enough to be sure about that. There is not any doubt that the rate at which water is being used at the present time, particularly in highly settled areas like the old part of Ontario, and the gradual denuding of forest cover, have contributed to what may be a long term situation. Since this situation has been partly created by man, perhaps it will need man to do something to offset it.
I would be hopeful that the ARDA program would have some effect in helping in the conservation of water. We are going to have to look quite seriously at this. With respect to some of the streams that were diverted into lake Superior, the diversions were started about a generation ago, and perhaps steps no one would have once contemplated even a very few years ago will have to be studied.
I do not think there is any possibility of doing too much research into this problem.

More and more we come to realize, not only all over this continent but throughout the world that water, which seems in many respects to be the cheapest commodity of all, is the most precious resource we have.
Speaking for myself, and I think for those of my colleagues who have a special responsibility in this matter, I will endeavour to see that everything is done that can be done to study the long term problem. Certainly we intend to do everything possible to alleviate

and I am afraid it can only be to alleviate

the immediate situation which is a cause of very great concern-perhaps of greater concern in Georgian bay than anywhere else- but of great concern to the whole of the lakes region.
TION or DEEP WATER PORT

Mr. Speaker, if I insisted on raising the question of the construction of a sea harbour at Riviere du Loup, it is because representations were made to me by people of great experience in matters of navigation on the St. Lawrence river. They are shipmasters who spend all their lives on the river and know it practically through and through.
Their experience acquired over many years of navigation on these waters gives them a knowledge that we do not have and could hardly acquire even with the most competent government engineers. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what those people say? Well, they maintain that to build a sea harbour at Riviere du Loup at the cost of $7 million would be a mere waste of money, and that they cannot understand how qualified engineers could recommend such an expenditure, which will be a true waste of public funds. It is so evident that one already wonders whether that undue expenditure of public funds, if it is made will not be a typical example of plain patronage such as practised by the Union Nationale, but this time at the federal government level.
To support these statements, let me tell you that to build a sea harbour in Riviere du Loup, it would be necessary in the first place to dig deeply into the bottom of the river and to maintain it at a reasonable depth it would have to be dredged throughout the year. Then in the winter, on account of the general direction of winds, that sea harbour would be so heavily ice-bound that it would be necessary to have at least two or three icebreakers to clear it.
I would be glad for Riviere du Loup if an ocean port were established there, but it is not my fault if common sense and economic 20220-172

On the other hand, in the county of Charlevoix, two places are wonderfully suited to serve as ocean ports: Baie St. Paul and Pointe au Pic.
In addition, mineral resources are far greater on the north shore. At the present time, the economic slump is more severe in Charlevoix. Finally, the places mentioned have the natural qualities and meet the standards required for ocean ports. That is why it would be a tragic mistake for the Minister of Transport to go and spend $7 million where such an expenditure would be practically useless.
I suggest, therefore, that the minister be very cautious with this bill and give it full consideration before going ahead with it; incidentally, I would ask him to consider all the possibilities which Baie St. Paul or Pointe au Pic offer for a bill of this scope.
Furthermore, the establishment of a sea port at Riviere du Loup would not bring any great changes in the economy of that place, for Riviere du Loup does not suffer from lack of means of transportation; it already has the trans-Canada highway, and the C.N.R. as well as enough wharves for current business, and its economy at the present time is far more developed than that of Charlevoix county. In any case, such a harbour could not stay open all winter long, even if a lot of money were spent to keep it clear of ice.
Furthermore, it is precisely because the south shore was always favoured that part of the traffic going to the north shore passes on the other side of the river for quite a distance.
Besides, and nobody can deny this, since facts are there to prove it-it is on the north shore that one finds mining and other resources. In the long run, good sense will have to prevail; it is on the north shore that seaports and wharves should be built.
That is why I feel that the government would do well to start reversing that trend right now and stop favouring the south shore at the expense of the north shore.
Mr. Speaker, if I have chosen to speak of the riding of Charlevoix and of the harbour of Riviere du Loup, it is not so much to try to get a little more work for my riding-even though that would be commendable-but rather because I feel it is wasteful to make an expenditure of $7 million at a place where it would be useless, especially considering the deficits accumulated by the present government.
